Round 773 — the quest seam, and the same.decision_summary:
R773 (BUILD, engine, no store change) — the JOURNAL axis gets the seam the narrative axis got in R769, because the consumer's second lift request asks for the emitter that sits on top of it and there is nothing under it yet. `QuestProjection` had no plain-data shape, and it could not have one by accident: `QuestView`, `QuestWorldView` and `QuestCompletionView` are `#[non_exhaustive]`, so generated code in another crate cannot construct one. That is the same wall `LinePart` and `CastPart` were built for, and the answer is the same — `QuestProjectionParts` with `QuestPart` / `QuestWorldPart` / `QuestCompletionPart`, `to_parts` to emit, and a `from_parts` that takes no `Result` because the quest-graph read and the precondition join already ran.

THE SAME DOOR WAS OPEN HERE, AND CLOSED THE SAME WAY. `quest.rs` opens by saying every quest is store-derived and the kernel invents none, "so a consumer's quest list cannot drift from the store". `QuestProjection::from_report` was public and takes a `QuestGraphReport`, which is a pub-field struct — so a downstream crate could hand the kernel quests the store never declared and get `QuestView`s back, and the module's opening promise was false in exactly the way R764 found the crate's headline promise false on the narrative axis. R771 fixed the one; this fixes the twin. It is worth naming that the twin existed at all: R771's entry closed "the mnemosyne half of this arc is DONE", and it was, for the axis being worked. The identical hole one module over went unlooked-at because nothing was pulling on it yet.

PROVEN BY A PAIR, NOT BY A LONE compile_fail. The negative doctest is preceded by a positive one using the same path spelling, so a typo cannot fake the guard — R771's argument, reused because it is right and because a second axis is exactly where an argument gets copied badly.

WHAT DOES NOT MOVE TO THE BUILD. The completability gate stays where it is. R764 said quest preconditions are game rules over player state and stay at runtime, and the consumer's own request agreed with that sentence while asking for something else: the DERIVATION of the projection, not the EVALUATION of its rules. So `QuestProjectionParts` carries no gate result, and the equivalence test insists a baked projection can still ANSWER the gate — it builds a two-road world where one road digs the precondition in time and the other never does, asserts the verdict has length one, and only then asserts live and baked agree. Two empty vectors comparing equal would have proven nothing.

`to_parts` SORTS NOTHING, and that is documented rather than left to be rediscovered as a bug. The playable seam sorts because the projection holds `HashMap`s; this one holds a `Vec` the graph derived from a `BTreeSet` and a `BTreeMap` per world, with preconditions sorted and deduped at ingestion. Determinism is inherited, and saying so is cheaper than a future round wondering whether the omission was an oversight.

The completability gate is NOT baked, which is the line R764 drew and this round keeps: a precondition evaluated against player state is a game rule that stays at runtime; what moves to the build is the DERIVATION of the quest layer

The equivalence test asserts the gate agrees on a REAL verdict (one violation on the road that never digs the clue), not on two empty vectors — a baked quest layer that could not still answer the gate would be useless

THE SAME DOOR WAS OPEN HERE, AND CLOSED THE SAME WAY. `quest.rs` opens by saying every quest is store-derived and the kernel invents none, "so a consumer's quest list cannot drift from the store". `QuestProjection::from_report` was public and takes a `QuestGraphReport`, which is a pub-field struct — so a downstream crate could hand the kernel quests the store never declared and get `QuestView`s back, and the module's opening promise was false in exactly the way R764 found the crate's headline promise false on the narrative axis. R771 fixed the one; this fixes the twin. It is worth naming that the twin existed at all: R771's entry closed "the mnemosyne half of this arc is DONE", and it was, for the axis being worked. The identical hole one module over went unlooked-at because nothing was pulling on it yet.

PROVEN BY A PAIR, NOT BY A LONE compile_fail. The negative doctest is preceded by a positive one using the same path spelling, so a typo cannot fake the guard — R771's argument, reused because it is right and because a second axis is exactly where an argument gets copied badly.

WHAT DOES NOT MOVE TO THE BUILD. The completability gate stays where it is. R764 said quest preconditions are game rules over player state and stay at runtime, and the consumer's own request agreed with that sentence while asking for something else: the DERIVATION of the projection, not the EVALUATION of its rules. So `QuestProjectionParts` carries no gate result, and the equivalence test insists a baked projection can still ANSWER the gate — it builds a two-road world where one road digs the precondition in time and the other never does, asserts the verdict has length one, and only then asserts live and baked agree. Two empty vectors comparing equal would have proven nothing.

`to_parts` SORTS NOTHING, and that is documented rather than left to be rediscovered as a bug. The playable seam sorts because the projection holds `HashMap`s; this one holds a `Vec` the graph derived from a `BTreeSet` and a `BTreeMap` per world, with preconditions sorted and deduped at ingestion. Determinism is inherited, and saying so is cheaper than a future round wondering whether the omission was an oversight.

Round 774 — the quest emitter, and the s.decision_summary:
R774 (BUILD, engine-build, no store change) — the consumer's second lift request, answered. `emit_quest_projection` is the sibling of `emit_playable_projection`: it projects the quest graph at build time and returns Rust source defining `quest_projection() -> QuestProjection`. With both emitters in hand, a consumer that bakes both never opens the store at startup, which is the whole of the owner's directive rather than the half the first emitter bought — the consumer measured that half exactly: 3.5 billion instructions removed from `Narrative::load` and a nearly identical 3.5 billion still standing next to it in `Knots::load`.

THE REQUEST DID NOT ARGUE WITH R764 AND NEITHER DOES THIS. R764 wrote that quest preconditions are game rules over player state and stay at runtime. The request quoted that sentence back and said it is asking for something else: the DERIVATION of the projection, not the EVALUATION of its rules. That distinction is exactly right and it is the shape built here. `QuestProjectionParts` carries no gate result, and a baked projection still answers `completability` against a playable projection whenever it is asked, because the gate is a question, not a field.

ONE THING THE EMITTER DELIBERATELY CANNOT DO. `QuestProjection::from_workspace` takes an order override; this takes none and passes `None`. An `--order` override is CWD-relative CLI semantics with no meaning in a build script, and worse, it would read a canon order this crate did not declare to cargo — the exact divergence between the file declared and the file opened that R772 closed two rounds ago. The right fix for a footgun found once is to leave no way to hold it, not to write a warning next to it.

THE RENDERER IS ONE TEXT, NOT TWO. `render_quest` shares the quoter, the vec helper and the `Option` helper with `render`, so the claim that `{:?}` on a `&str` is exactly Rust literal escaping is proven once for both axes and cannot be fixed on one and missed on the other. The quest fixture is compiled by this crate's own `build.rs` on the same terms as the playable one — all three `QuestState` variants, a completion with an actor and one without, a quest spanning two roads, and the nasty string in an objective, because a quest objective is authored prose and quotes as freely as a line does.

THE DOWNSTREAM CHECK IS REPEATED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. Every `QuestView` type is `#[non_exhaustive]`, so a struct literal for one fails to compile outside `mnemosyne-engine` — and R773's round-trip test lives INSIDE that crate and structurally cannot see it. That is precisely how the R769 defect survived until R770 caught it from here. So this crate, which is downstream, builds a `QuestProjectionParts` by literal; if the parts type ever readmits a member no foreign crate can construct, this stops compiling.

VERIFIED AGAINST THE LIVE STORE, NOT ONLY FIXTURES. The emitter was run on the consumer's real workspace: 45,060 bytes of source out, compiled, and the baked projection compared EQUAL to the live one across all 22 real quests — all seven knots present, seven quests carrying `opened_by` preconditions. The same run confirmed R772 end to end, resolving the consumer's own `mnemosyne.toml`, `canon-order.json` and `.atomic/tide.atomic.json`, where R770's declaration had named a store that does not exist in that workspace.

Round 775 — one body was the cost, not o.decision_summary:
R775 (BUILD, engine-build, no store change) — the consumer filed a measurement it explicitly declined to turn into a request: the baked playable source is 2.6MB in 18 lines, 98% of it a single nested `from_parts` expression, and it did not ask for a change because it had not measured any alternative's compile time. That is the right discipline and it left the question with the party holding the emitter. So it was measured here.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENT SAYS. The cost is FUNCTION BODY SIZE. Not line length, not total volume, not nesting as such. A controlled pair settles it: the same element literals, the same types, byte counts within 0.4%, differing only in whether they sit in one function or a hundred — 5,000 elements took 29.1s and 1.21GB of rustc in one body and 5.5s and 0.57GB in a hundred. And it is superlinear, so it worsens as a store grows: the same one-body encoding at 2,500 elements took 9.0s, meaning 2x the input cost 3.2x the time.

SO THE EMITTER SPLITS BODIES AND KEEPS THE TYPES. Every list it writes, at every depth, becomes chunk functions of at most 50 literals; the top-level function holds one call per chunk — the structure, never the prose. On the consumer's real store that is 34.5s and 1.13GB before, 6.3s and 0.55GB after, with the longest line falling from 2,623,420 bytes to 26,816 across 520 chunk functions. The file grew 1.6%, paid once for a 5.3x compile win. The regenerated source was compiled and compared EQUAL to the live projection — 66 sections, 799 lines — because a faster bake that is a different bake is not a win.

THE PROPOSED REMEDY WAS NOT NEEDED, AND SAYING SO IS THE POINT. The consumer sketched a flat `&'static [(&str, &str)]` table plus an index, reasoning that it would parse near-linearly. It would — and it would give up the type checking that is the entire reason the bake is Rust source and not JSON (R764 rejected `Deserialize` precisely because a serialized snapshot cannot carry a shape contract). The measurement shows that trade was never necessary: the same win is available without touching the typing. A hypothesis can be right about the SYMPTOM and wrong about the remedy, and the way to tell is to measure rather than to reason from the sketch.

ONE FINDING THAT ONLY THE NEW ENCODING COULD PRODUCE. Generated FUNCTIONS have signatures, and a signature is a lint surface the old single expression never had — `clippy::type_complexity` rejects the expanded four-level `by_world` element type, in the generated file, in a consumer's build, under the `-D warnings` a consumer is entitled to run. Found by this workspace's own fixture compile, which is the reason that fixture is compiled by `build.rs` at all, and fixed at the cause with the kernel's existing `SectionLines` alias rather than an allow. A generator whose output does not survive its consumer's lints has not finished generating.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED. 50 is the chunk the measurement used, not a tuned optimum; no sweep was run, and the finding is that a BOUND must exist, not that this is the best one. The generated file's RUNTIME cost is untouched and unmeasured here — it still allocates a `String` per quoted value at startup — and interning would be a separate round with its own numbers.

Round 776 — a world it cannot see is not.decision_summary:
R776 (BUILD/DEBT, mnemosyne-engine, no store change) — the owner asked whether the default engine had a problem. A review of the crate found two, both of the same shape: a FAIL-LOUD GATE THAT ANSWERS A QUESTION IT CANNOT SEE WITH THE WORD FOR SAFE. This round fixes the playable one; the quest one is the next round.

WHAT WAS WRONG. `PlayableProjection::gate(world)` opens by taking `self.walk(world)`, which returns an empty slice for a world the projection does not carry. The loop that produces every finding then never runs, and the function returns an empty vec — which the same doc comment defines as "the interactive layer is play-clean". So a typo'd, stale, or foreign world name did not fail; it PASSED. This was measured before it was fixed rather than argued from the code: on one projection, `gate("main")` returned its real EmptySpot finding and `gate("mian")` returned nothing.

WHY IT SURVIVED, WHICH IS THE MORE USEFUL HALF. The kernel held the authoritative world set privately and exposed no way to ask for it. `by_world`, `walks` and `forks` are all private and there was no enumerator anywhere in the public API, so a consumer wanting to gate every road had to bring its own list. The first consumer did exactly that: it rebuilt the list by walking the fork graph from `main` through `walk` and `forks_at`. That is a DIFFERENT definition — "fork-reachable from the trunk" instead of "carried by this projection" — and a registered world-line that no fork edge points at would simply never have been gated, with nothing anywhere able to say so. This is the mistake R766 refused to make on the prose axis, where the slicer exposes `in_prose_order()` precisely so an ordered caller never re-implements the search and drifts from it. The world set had no such door, so the caller re-implemented it. On today's store the two definitions happen to coincide at seven worlds, which is worth saying plainly: the defect is structural rather than currently-manifesting, and the reason it is worth paying now is that nothing would report it if they diverged.

THE FIX IS TWO THINGS, AND THEY BELONG TOGETHER. `worlds()` returns the projection's own world list, sorted, so the question can be asked. `GateViolation::UnknownWorld` is what `gate` returns, alone, when it is asked about a world it does not carry — alone because with no walk the remaining checks would each spend themselves on emptiness and hand back the clean verdict, which is the bug wearing a longer form.

THE PREDICATE IS THE WORLD MAP, NOT THE WALK'S LENGTH, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE CARE OF THIS ROUND. `walks` holds an entry for every world in the report, so a REGISTERED world whose walk is empty is known with nothing on it, while an unknown name has no entry at all. Those are different facts and they deserve different answers: the first is a clean verdict honestly earned, the second is a question the gate cannot answer. Spelled the lazy way — `walk(world).is_empty()` — they collapse into one answer that is wrong for both, turning every empty-but-real world into a fabricated violation while the actual defect stays half-fixed. A test pins both directions on one projection so the distinction cannot be optimised away later.

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY LEFT ALONE. The read accessors — `lines`, `walk`, `cast_at`, `scene`, `live_doors_at` — still answer empty for an unknown world, and their docs already say so. The line drawn here is not "emptiness is bad": an accessor that says "nothing here" has answered, while a GATE that says "clean" has issued a verdict about something it never examined. Only the verdict was changed.

ONE SMALL THING FOUND WHILE FIXING IT. The baked-equivalence test — the one that proves a projection survives `to_parts`/`from_parts` — iterated a hand-written `["main", "dark"]`. That is the same hand-list mistake in miniature, inside the test whose job is to prove the artifact, where a world added to the fixture would silently stop being checked. It now derives the list from `worlds()`.

New `GateViolation::UnknownWorld`, returned alone and nothing else: with no walk there is nothing the remaining checks could examine, so continuing would spend each of them on emptiness and hand back the clean verdict

New `PlayableProjection::worlds()` — the authoritative world set, sorted; it existed only privately, so the first consumer rebuilt the list by walking the fork graph from `main` through `walk` + `forks_at`, which is the different definition "fork-reachable from the trunk" rather than "carried by this projection"

The membership test is the world MAP, not `walk(world).is_empty()`: a registered world whose walk is empty is KNOWN and honestly clean, an unknown name is a question the gate cannot answer, and the lazy spelling collapses both into one answer that is wrong for both

Read accessors deliberately keep answering empty for an unknown world (`lines`, `walk`, `cast_at`, `scene`, `live_doors_at`): an accessor that says "nothing here" is an answer, a gate that says "clean" is a verdict, and the line drawn is the verdict rather than the emptiness

Round 777 — the gate covered sixteen of.decision_summary:
R777 (BUILD/DEBT, mnemosyne-validate + mnemosyne-cli + mnemosyne.toml) — R776's commit printed the citation gate's own report on the way past, and `mnemosyne-engine` was not in its scanned path list. It had never been. Neither had `mnemosyne-engine-build`, `mnemosyne-render`, or `mnemosyne-plugin-tree-sitter-cpp`.

WHAT THAT MEANT. `[plugins.set_equality_validator].paths` was a HAND LIST of sixteen sibling directories, and the tree has twenty. CLAUDE.md tells every agent, in the citation-hygiene section, that a `Round NNN` in `crates/*/src/` is checked by `validate-code-refs` on every commit. That sentence was false for four crates — including the one that R756 through R776 had been landing in, a dozen consecutive rounds of dense `Round NNN` annotation, none of it gated. The written contract was right about the intent; the config simply could not express it, so it restated it by hand and then drifted.

THIS IS R772 AGAIN, ONE LAYER DOWN, WHICH IS THE POINT WORTH KEEPING. R772 found `cargo:rerun-if-changed` naming a hand-written store path that was not the store the bake read, and drew the rule: the oracle is the resolver, never a hand list, because a hand list is a copy of the bug class. Five rounds later the same shape was sitting in the config of the validator whose entire job is catching claims that have quietly stopped being true. A list restates the tree and then diverges from it IN SILENCE, because a path merely absent from the list looks exactly like a path deliberately excluded — there is no reading of the file that distinguishes the two.

THE FIX DERIVES THE SET. `walk_paths` now accepts `*` as a whole path segment, and the config is one line: `crates/*/src/`. A crate is gated the day it exists. `*/src/` still leaves `tests/` out, which is the R264 policy decision recorded above it in the config, not an oversight the pattern should quietly reverse. The hidden/`target`/`node_modules` skip predicate was extracted to one function and is read both when descending and when expanding, because two copies would let a `*` scan what a walk skips.

THE PAYOFF ARRIVED IMMEDIATELY, WHICH IS WHAT A GATE IS FOR. Widening the scan surfaced six real violations, all in the engine, all the same: `§5` written to mean "section 5 of a tide field report". In this codebase `§` is a STORE SECTION id and the gate resolves it as one, so every one of those was a reject that no run had ever performed. They are rewritten as `sec 5`, which is the convention COMMIT_FORMAT already carries for design-doc references, for exactly this reason.

AND THE REPORT NOW SHOWS COVERAGE RATHER THAN CONFIGURATION. `scanned_paths` printed `cfg.paths` — it echoed its own input, which is why four missing crates could hide behind a report that looked complete. It now prints the EXPANDED list (twenty directories today) beside the configured pattern, resolved through the same `expand_paths` the walk itself uses, so the printed answer cannot drift from the scanned one either.

ONE DEBT THIS ROUND CREATED, PAID IN IT. A pattern makes a new vacuity reachable: an older installed binary without `*` support reads `crates/*/src/` as a literal path, finds nothing, scans nothing, and reports zero violations — the same clean a clean tree reports. So an entirely-unresolvable scan set is now an error rather than an empty walk. SOME configured path missing stays silently skipped, which is the deliberate optional-checkout behaviour; ALL of them missing is a validator with no file to read, and that must not be spelled the same way as success. The CLI was reinstalled before this commit for the same reason.
changes_bullets: The code-citation gate's configured path list was a hand list of sixteen sibling directories against a tree of twenty, so mnemosyne-engine, mnemosyne-engine-build, mnemosyne-render and mnemosyne-plugin-tree-sitter-cpp were never scanned — including the crate a dozen consecutive rounds had been landing in, while CLAUDE.md told every agent the gate covered `crates/*/src/`

`walk_paths` accepts `*` as a whole path segment and the config becomes the one line `crates/*/src/`, so the scanned set is DERIVED from the tree and a new crate is gated the day it exists — the R772 rule (the oracle is the resolver, a hand list is a copy of the bug class) applied to the validator's own config

Widening the scan immediately surfaced six real violations, all in the engine and all the same one: `§5` written to mean section 5 of a tide FIELD REPORT, where `§` in this codebase is a store section id the gate resolves as one; rewritten as `sec 5`, the convention COMMIT_FORMAT already carries for design-doc refs

`scanned_paths` in the report was `cfg.paths` — it echoed its own input, which is how four missing crates hid behind a report that looked complete; it now prints the EXPANDED coverage beside the configured pattern, resolved through the same `expand_paths` the walk uses

A scan set where EVERY configured path resolves to nothing is now an error rather than an empty walk: a validator with no file to read reports the same clean a clean tree reports, and a pattern makes that newly reachable through an older binary that reads `crates/*/src/` as a literal path
Some configured path missing stays silently skipped, unchanged — that is the deliberate declare-intent-for-optional-checkouts behaviour, and only the all-missing case is a fault
The hidden / `target` / `node_modules` skip predicate moved into one function read by both the descent and the `*` expansion, because two copies would let a pattern scan what a walk refuses

Round 778 — the pair nothing was checkin.decision_summary:
R778 (BUILD/DEBT, mnemosyne-engine, no store change) — the sibling of R776, and the second half of the review the owner asked for. The playable gate answered an unknown world with the word for clean; the quest gate did the same thing one axis over, and for a reason R776's fix did not reach.

WHAT WAS WRONG. `QuestProjection::completability(&PlayableProjection)` takes the deadline for each road as the earliest completion scene's position on that road's walk. A world the playable projection does not carry has an empty walk, so no position is found, so there is no deadline, so the road was `continue`d — silently. Every precondition on that road went unchecked and the gate returned no finding about it, which is indistinguishable from having checked it and found nothing. Measured before it was fixed rather than argued from the code: one quest layer declaring a road called `braid`, paired with a playable projection that knows only `main`, returned an empty vec; paired with one that walks `braid`, the same layer returned the real precondition violation.

THE DEEPER PROBLEM IS THAT NOTHING JOINED THE PAIR. These are two independently built projections. Each carries the `telling` it was resolved under; neither ever looked at the other's. Each constructor takes `telling` as its own argument, and a build-time bake makes that TWO separate emitter invocations (R774), so producing a mismatched pair required no mistake more exotic than typing a different string twice. The first consumer already hands the two DIFFERENT overrides — precondition predicates to the quest side, defaults to the playable side — so the pairing was loose in practice before it was loose in theory.

WHAT IT DOES NOW. A pair cut for different tellings is `TellingMismatch`, returned ALONE: every finding underneath would be a statement about the wrong world, and a list of those reads as work done. A quest road the playable projection does not carry is `WorldNotWalked` naming the quest that lost its check, rather than a skipped iteration.

THE STRICTNESS WAS SET BY MEASUREMENT, NOT BY TASTE. Before writing a check that can fail a real store, both world sets were read off the first consumer's store: `report-playable-world` and `report-quest-graph` under `reader` return the same seven names, and both report nine registered branches, the difference being the three `weave-*` confluences that neither projection carries as a world. So the new violation cannot fire there, and its non-vacuity comes from injection in a test instead — which is the right source, because a check that fires on a correct store is a check that will be deleted.

ONE THING CORRECTED RATHER THAN FIXED, SAID PLAINLY. A comment here claimed that because a withheld fact emits no line, "offered" is exactly "diggable under this telling". That is false whenever a consumer declares `journal_predicates`: the projection routes typed journal facts OUT of the line stream, so a precondition fact that is itself a typed leg is offered by the store and invisible to this gate, which would report it unreachable when it is not. The direction is a false alarm rather than a silent pass, and no consumer pairs a journal-routing playable projection with this gate today, so the behaviour is left alone and the sentence is not. "Offered" here means "disclosed as prose". Making the gate see the store's offer rather than the consumer's prose stream needs an accessor that does not exist and a decision about what offered should mean, which is a round, not a clause.

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT ADDED. A quest whose completion beats all sit off its world's walk still yields no deadline and is still not gated. That is a different defect — a store inconsistency rather than a mispaired projection — and the first consumer's store demonstrably carries quests that are Done on a road with no completion beat at all, a neighbourhood this round did not characterise. Turning it red without measuring it is how a gate earns its reputation for being wrong.

Round 779 — a shared rule one caller cou.decision_summary:
R779 (BUILD/DEBT, mnemosyne-engine + mnemosyne-render, no store change) — the third and last confirmed finding of the review that produced R776 and R778, and the one whose fix makes a sentence already written in this crate true.

WHAT WAS WRONG. `PlayableProjection::scene` bundled a spot as a `SceneView` and filled its `doors` from the UNFILTERED `doors_at`, while `live_doors_at` filtered the same doors through the disclose-freshness rule. Two public read paths to one datum, under two different invariants. R762/R763 built that rule precisely so the tide field-report dead-door class could not recur, and recorded that its strength was being a SHARED RULE rather than a gate — one definition every disclose-door calls, so the half-enforced-invariant class is structurally impossible. It was not shared. It was available, and the accessor a renderer reaches for first declined it.

The doc on `live_doors_at` said, in as many words, that the dead-door class "cannot recur through the kernel's own doors". That was false while `scene` existed in its old shape, and it was false in the most expensive way a doc comment can be: it described the guarantee a reader would rely on instead of writing their own check.

WHAT IT DOES NOW. `scene` takes `known` and builds its doors through `live_doors_at`. There is one path. A reader with no session state passes an empty set, which filters nothing — freshness is a set difference — but states "this reader holds nothing" rather than leaving the question unasked. The engine's own text renderer does exactly that in `render_playthrough`, where it is not a workaround but the truth: a playthrough rendering lays out the whole declared walk at once, so there is no reader partway through it holding anything.

WHY A SIGNATURE CHANGE RATHER THAN A DOC FIX. The two-path shape was the defect, so a doc that described it accurately would have preserved it. The old call is exactly recoverable — `scene(w, s, &HashSet::new())` — so nothing is lost but the ability to skip the rule by accident, and the cost falls entirely inside this workspace: the first consumer never called `scene`, building its own doors and calling `fresh_disclosure` itself, which is why this was latent rather than live.

THE TEST IS THE POINT, NOT THE EDIT. The assertion is that `scene(...).doors` EQUALS `live_doors_at(...)` at every `known` the surrounding test already establishes — nothing known, one fact known, both known. A future short-cut back to the unfiltered set now fails in this crate rather than in a consumer's chrome. Non-vacuity was proven by injection rather than by reading: putting `doors_at` back makes the assertion fail on the both-known case, which was run.

Round 780 — the axis the emitter's own g.decision_summary:
R780 (BUILD/DEBT, mnemosyne-engine-build, no store change) — the first consumer's third field report returned a measurement of Round 775 on a store larger than any fixture here, and reported an axis that round had also fixed without knowing it: before it, the baked artifact compiled at cargo's DEFAULT dev profile aborted at run time with `fatal runtime error: stack overflow`. This round builds the gate that was missing.

WHAT WAS NOT MEASURED. When the whole store is one function body holding one nested expression, every temporary in it is live until the expression ends and each gets its own slot, so the frame grows with the store until it exceeds the thread's stack. Round 775 removed that shape and measured the win in COMPILE time. Nothing here would have noticed the runtime half either way: this crate's fixtures are two lines long, and the Round 775 regression test weighs the emitted TEXT, never a running artifact. A property whose only evidence is that a different property held is not gated — it is inferred, and it stops being true silently.

WHAT IS ASSERTED, AND WHY NONE OF IT IS A THRESHOLD. A byte figure is fitted to today's store and turns a gate into an argument about the constant. The claim is a RATIO — the artifact must cost the same stack at four times the size — the Round 775 scaling assertion moved from the emitted text to the running artifact. A ratio has its own failure mode: "did not grow" is also what a broken measurement says. So the same test measures a CONTROL, the identical parts emitted with the bound removed, and requires it to GROW. One test rather than two, because that arm licenses the others: split apart, the flat arms could report green while the instrument sat broken in another test's red.

THAT IS ROUNDS 776 THROUGH 779 IN CONSTRUCTIVE FORM. Those rounds removed three gates that returned the word for SAFE about input they could not examine. The way not to write a fourth is not to check more carefully; it is to make the gate demonstrate, on every run, that it can see. `render_bounded` exists for exactly that — the bound is a value rather than a constant read so the control can be EMITTED, and without it non-vacuity could only have been a comment claiming someone checked once.

MEASURED, AND ONE PREDICTION CORRECTED. Playable 32 KiB at both sizes, quest 28 KiB at both, control 96 KiB then 344 KiB. Injecting the bound removal back into the emitter put both shipped artifacts on the control's curve and turned every assertion red, which was run and then reverted. The correction: optimization does NOT fold the growth away, as this round first assumed and wrote down. At opt-level 3 the control still wants 44 KiB then 160 KiB — the same 3.6x — while the shipped artifact sits at 4 KiB flat. So the consumer's `[profile.dev] opt-level = 1` never made the pre-Round-775 artifact safe. It halved a cost that grows with the store, which only doubles the size at which the abort arrives. The crash was scheduled, not avoided, and this gate is profile-independent as a result.

Round 781 — two artifacts that could not.decision_summary:
R781 (DEBT, mnemosyne-engine-build, no store change) — Round 774 opened a second emitter beside the first, and Round 775 gave both a chunk-function naming scheme that restarts its counter at zero on every render. So the two artifacts define the same private names, and splicing them into one module is E0428 once per chunk. The first consumer found it; this workspace could not.

WHY IT COULD NOT. Every include! here already sat in a module of its own — two in the lib tests, six in the stack probe — so the arrangement that fails was the one arrangement nothing built. That is the Rounds 776-780 class one step further out again: not a gate answering blind, and not a property with no gate, but a property whose gate was arranged so it could never disagree. The crate docs meanwhile describe the failing arrangement, two include! snippets presented as the same shape and compiled apart by rustdoc, so a consumer following them verbatim gets the collision.

THE WALL IS A MODULE, AND ITS NAME IS DERIVED. The consumer suggested a per-emitter prefix. A prefix is a constant picked per emitter, which is a hand list a third emitter can silently fail to extend, and Round 777 removed exactly that shape from this workspace's own config. The module name comes from the public item the artifact defines instead, and two artifacts must already define different public items to compose at all — so the wall is distinct exactly when composition is possible, including for an emitter nobody has written. Both emitters end in one shared assembler rather than each writing its own tail, so the rule cannot hold on one axis and quietly not on the other.

THE GATE IS THE ARRANGEMENT. The lib's two separate baked modules collapse into one holding both artifacts, making the composition a build failure here rather than downstream. A compile-time claim is also what two empty files satisfy, so the non-vacuity arm sits in the same file: both artifacts are asserted to define __mn_0, and the wall is asserted as a difference between their module lines rather than against their spellings. Injecting the pre-round shape reproduced the consumer's error byte for byte.

AND A PREDICTION THIS ROUND MADE WAS WRONG. The first draft of the rationale argued the module beats a prefix because a prefix lengthens the reassembly expression, the longest line in the file. Measurement says it is not: at 800 lines the longest line is a chunk body at 15,120 bytes against a reassembly of 332, so neither choice moves the quantity Round 775 gates. The derivation argument stands alone; the cost argument was rewritten to the figures.

Round 783 — the gate's own reach was a h.decision_summary:
R783 (BUILD/DEBT, mnemosyne-validate + mnemosyne-ops + mnemosyne-config, no store change) — Round 777 removed a hand list of sixteen scan directories and derived the set with `crates/*/src/`, on the grounds that a list restates the tree and then drifts from it in silence. That fixed the drift one level down. One level up, the glob is itself a claim about which TREES hold citations, and it had gone stale the same silent way.

WHAT WAS OUTSIDE. Fourteen files of production code: every `crates/*/build.rs` — including the emitter's own build script that the last five rounds have been editing — and all ten of `tools/*/src/`. CLAUDE.md tells every agent the citation gate covers this workspace, and for those files it did not.

THE FIX IS NOT ANOTHER PATH. Another path would be the same shape of claim, correct until the next tree appears. `scan_coverage` walks every Rust source under the root and requires each to be either covered by a configured path or named in a new `scan_exclusions` list, and `validate-workspace` fails on anything in neither. The failure mode inverts: a tree merely absent is loud, and only a tree someone wrote down stays quiet. A declared exclusion matching no file is reported as stale, the rule the orphan-ledger axis already applies to a row whose orphan resolved, so the list cannot rot into folklore that still reads as policy.

NO ALLOW-LIST WAS BUILT. What blocked this extension for two rounds was two citations in the server's build script naming pre-252 rounds, off-main and unverifiable by construction, with no mechanism to register them. Building that mechanism would have institutionalised precisely what the gate exists to prevent; and unlike a frozen ledger entry, a comment can simply be corrected. The anchors were deleted and their substance kept.

WHAT THE ROUND FOUND AND COULD NOT FIX. `studio/` was scanned briefly and it took one pass to surface three design-doc references written as section-id citations. Staging any edit there makes the pre-commit hook build that workspace, and it does not compile: this workspace's own `list_changelog` changed shape under it, and so did a pinion trait it implements. The pinion half cannot be repaired while that sibling repository is mid-flight, so `studio/` is declared as an exclusion — which is this round's own thesis applied to its own shortfall. The omission is written down instead of silent.

Round 785 — the handle they did not ask.decision_summary:
R785 (DESIGN, code 0, no store change) — the first consumer's field report asked for projection types that can hold `&'static` instead of owning `String`, and their reply named the constraint that actually decides the shape: not whether the FIELD is a `Cow`, but what LIFETIME the accessor returns. With `fn text(&self) -> &str` they keep copying regardless of the field, because the accessor borrows `&self` and their struct holds the projection, so borrowing would be self-referential.

THE REFRAME. The larger half of their win needs no type change at all. `pub fn text(&self) -> &str` desugars to `fn text<'s>(&'s self) -> &'s str`, so a `&'static` projection already yields `&'static str` from today's unmodified accessors. What blocks them is not the signature; it is that the baked entry point hands back a value they must own. This was compile-checked against the current engine rather than reasoned about: a probe feeding five accessors from a `&'static PlayableProjection` into functions accepting only `&'static str` and `&'static [String]` builds clean.

THE LADDER. Step 1: the baked emitter returns `&'static PlayableProjection` from a `OnceLock`. No kernel change, `from_workspace` untouched, and the consumer's second copy of 4,612 lines stops being forced. Step 2: `Cow<'static, str>` fields — Owned from the workspace, Borrowed from the emitted literal — which is the arm Round 782 measured at 99.5% fewer allocation calls and 5.5x cheaper to compile, with `Cow` kept an implementation detail so scalar accessors still return `&str`.

STEP 3 IS REJECTED. Chunk statics under a static of slices reach zero allocations and 8.6x compile, and are the only rung that cannot be one type: const construction admits no map, vector or string, and this projection holds five maps and a set, so the runtime constructor could not produce one. That means two projection types and a trait over them, permanently, in every consumer — a standing API tax for a residual measured in bytes that no consumer has been shown to need. Their own reply says what has value to them is building nothing at startup, not faster lookup, and steps 1 and 2 deliver that for everything they hold.

SEQUENCING. Step 1 alone first: the only rung needing no type change, the larger share of the win, and validatable against the consumer before any kernel type moves.

Round 786 — the handle, and the gate fig.decision_summary:
R786 (BUILD) — step 1 of the Round 785 ladder, and only step 1: the baked emitter's public item now hands back `&'static PlayableProjection` / `&'static QuestProjection` from a `OnceLock` instead of the projection by value. No kernel type moved, `from_workspace` is untouched, and no accessor signature changed — which is the whole point of putting this rung first. Lifetime elision already reads `pub fn text(&self) -> &str` as `fn text<'s>(&'s self) -> &'s str`, so a `&'static` receiver makes today's accessors yield `&'static str`, and `walk`, `spine` and `Line::entities` yield `&'static [String]`. What blocked the first consumer was never the signature it named; it was that the entry point handed back something they had to OWN, so reading out of the copy their struct held would have been self-referential and they transformed 4,612 lines into types of their own instead.

THE GATE. A test feeds real accessor output from BOTH baked artifacts into parameters that accept only `&'static`, so the property is a compile-time constraint rather than an assertion with a vacuous reading. Round 787 — what the audience is shown,.decision_summary: the completability gate read the prose stream to decide what the store OFFERS, so a precondition the consumer routes into its journal came back falsely unreachable; offered now means the store's offer, resolved in one place for both gates
changes_bullets: BUILD. Round 778 left this open in its own carry: `QuestProjection::completability` read the playable projection's PROSE stream to decide whether a completion-precondition fact was OFFERED in time, and a consumer's `journal_predicates` policy removes facts from that stream. So a precondition that is itself a typed journal leg is offered by the store and invisible to the gate, and came back as a FALSE `PreconditionUnreachable`

THE DECISION, which is what the carry was really waiting on: "offered" is the STORE's offer, not the consumer's prose. A fact is offered where the audience MEETS it — where it has a locator under this telling — and the journal policy decides only which STREAM carries it. The kernel now draws that split in one sentence: `lines` is what the audience is SHOWN, `offers` is what the audience can KNOW

Withholding still narrows it, which is the narrowing that was always intended rather than a side effect of reading the prose stream: a withheld fact emits no locator, so `offers` is false for it at every spot

`PlayableProjection::offers(world, section, fact_id)` is the new public accessor and the only public knowledge-axis surface. It answers `false` for an unknown world — an accessor saying "nothing here" is an answer, not a verdict (the Round 776 distinction), and a GATE still establishes the world separately

The journal-routed locators are RECORDED rather than dropped: a private `journal_offers` map, disjoint from `by_world` by construction, since a disclosed locator becomes a `Line` or lands there and never both. Empty for every consumer that declares no journal predicates

BOTH gates moved, not one. The ladder gate's G6 built its `earliest_offer` index from `lines` and had the identical defect on the identical question. Fixing only the quest gate would have left two public read paths over one datum with two invariants — the shape Round 779 removed for doors, recreated one layer up

One resolver, not two readings: a crate-private `offered_at` computes the union, `offers` is that plus a membership test, and G6's index is that scanned in walk order. The prose checks (G5 leak, G5 unreachable) deliberately stay on `lines`, because they ask what the ladder can SHOW

The seam carries it: `ProjectionParts.journal_offers` plus a `SectionJournalOffers` alias, emitted through the kernel's alias rather than a second spelling of the same type, so `from_workspace` and a bake answer the same question
verification_bullets: The defect was reproduced BEFORE it was fixed, the Round 776-779 method: a throwaway probe asserted the false `PreconditionUnreachable` and PASSED against the unfixed code, then failed against the fixed one with `left: []` against the finding it used to produce. The permanent tests are that probe with the corrected expectation

Both permanent tests are CONTROLLED TRIOS over one store where only the journal policy and one locator move. Arm 1: no journal policy, prose-disclosed in time, clean — without it the fixed arm would also pass on a gate that had simply stopped checking. Arm 2: the same fact routed to the journal, still met, clean. Arm 3 is the non-vacuity half — a precondition met only AT the completion scene (quest) or offered nowhere (ladder) still fires under the same policy

INJECTION 1 RAN: G6 reverted to reading `lines` fails `g6_a_journal_routed_precondition_is_known_in_time` on the routed arm alone, with the control and the non-vacuity arm still green. Reverted, green

INJECTION 2 RAN and FOUND A SECOND GAP rather than confirming a guess. The emitter made to drop `journal_offers` left `the_generated_source_rebuilds_the_projection_it_was_baked_from` GREEN — the engine's own round trip never goes through the emitter, so a silently dropped field looked exactly like an empty one. That is the Round 774 lesson recurring, and the assertion was added there, in the downstream crate, where it can see. Re-run under the same injection it fails; injection reverted, green

A FIELD ADDED TO `ProjectionParts` SILENTLY CHANGES WHY THE ROUND 786 `compile_fail` DOCTEST FAILS — it began failing with `E0063` (missing field) rather than the `E0597` it exists to assert. Caught because the POSITIVE arm of the pair is a build error and the negative one is not, which is the pair earning its keep. Re-checked the Round 786 way: extracted and compiled standalone against the engine rlib, exactly one error, and it is `E0597`

`Default` on `ProjectionParts` was CONSIDERED AND REJECTED as the fix for that fragility. It would make the doctest fixtures robust, but `..Default::default()` at a real construction site turns a forgotten field into a silent empty value — and the loud `E0063` is precisely what found all five construction sites in this round, including one in `mnemosyne-render` no test would have reached

Round 775's rule is that the emitted shape gets measured before it gets chosen, and they wrote the same expectation into the request

A FOURTH fixture family, `prose_fixtures`, weighed by the existing controlled-trio test rather than a second file: the counting allocator, the baseline discipline and the instrument-first arm are already there, and a second copy of a global allocator would be a second thing to drift

The arms mirror `Passage` field for field — the anchor's `source`, its `Prefix` locator, and the text — at the consumer's own coordinates, 56 spots of 2,655 characters, and its quadruple. Korean text, because a fixture in ASCII would price a third of the bytes it claims to

WHY A SEPARATE FAMILY RATHER THAN REUSING THE LINE PAIR: prose is the OPPOSITE shape. Round 782 weighed 4,612 strings of a few dozen characters; this is 56 strings of a few thousand. Reusing that pair would have measured the same shape twice and called the second one prose
verification_bullets: MEASURED, allocations at 56 spots then 224, in-test with the thread-local counting allocator: owned 171 then 680 allocations and 363,752 then 1,476,732 bytes; borrowed 3 then 8 allocations and 7,488 then 44,352 bytes

THE FIRST RESULT IS THAT ROUND 782's CONCLUSION DOES NOT CARRY. That round found borrowing removed 99.5% of the allocation calls and only 38% of the BYTES, and stated why: the strings were never the memory, the elements were. On prose the strings ARE the memory — borrowing cuts the bytes by 97.0%. Had this been assumed rather than measured, the design would have inherited a 38% figure that is wrong by a factor of two and a half on this axis

THE SECOND RESULT CONTRADICTS WHAT BOTH SIDES EXPECTED TO BE THE PROBLEM. The consumer's request warns that prose in one function body would repeat the very-long-expression trouble of Round 771, and it is right that the line is enormous: the longest emitted line is 319,510 bytes, twelve times the worst line in their current baked projection. It costs nothing. Compiling the whole 1.43 MB artifact is 0.05s of rustc user time against an empty-fixture baseline of 0.02s, with 30 MB of marginal peak RSS

THE COMPARISON THAT MAKES THAT READABLE, and the reason it is a finding rather than a small number: the line fixture at 4,612 items emits 1.34 MB and costs 2.47s. The prose fixture at 224 items emits 1.43 MB and costs 0.05s. Nearly the same bytes, roughly fifty times the compile cost, and what differs is the item count. Stated as a direction rather than an isolated variable, since the two families also differ in fields per item — but byte volume is plainly not the axis rustc charges for

SO THE ROUND 775 BOUND ALREADY HOLDS HERE AND THE EXISTING GATE ALREADY PASSES. `CHUNK` bounds ITEMS per body at 50, so a body holds at most 50 spots however many the store has, and the longest line is 319,510 bytes at 56 spots against 319,560 at 224 — flat. The Round 775 regression test asserts a RATIO rather than a byte threshold, which is exactly why a bake whose constant is twenty times larger than the projection's still satisfies it

The instrument is checked before it is read, the Round 780 discipline carried into this test: the owned arm must charge more at four times the prose, and must charge at least three allocations per spot, or the borrowed figures below it are vacuous. Both are asserted in the same test rather than in a comment

Compile figures are the median of three runs each, all six compilations exit 0 with zero rustc errors, checked by reading the real exit status rather than a filtered tail — the Round 782 lesson, which had already caught one silent failure earlier in this session

Round 790 — the door the line axis alrea.decision_summary: prose gets the same bake seam the projection has, because any bake door is a fabrication door and the line axis already made that trade unrecorded; the round's substance is saying so and correcting the three docs that hid it
changes_bullets: DESIGN, no code. Scratch: `claudedocs/passage-bake-design.md`. The first consumer's third lift request asks the kernel to bake its passages, and Round 789 removed two of the three things that could have decided the shape: compile cost is 0.05s for the whole artifact, and the 319 KB longest line is flat in store size because `CHUNK` bounds ITEMS, so the Round 775 gate already passes. One question was left and it is the forgery guard

THE GUARD, STATED CORRECTLY: the kernel cannot give generated code a privilege the consumer lacks. Generated source is spliced into the CONSUMER's crate, so anything it calls, a hand-written line in that crate calls. Any bake door is a fabrication door, and no sealed token, checksum or `#[doc(hidden)]` changes that — they narrow discoverability, not capability

AND THAT TRADE WAS ALREADY MADE, ON THE LINE AXIS, WITHOUT BEING WRITTEN DOWN. `Line`'s fields are crate-private and two `compile_fail` doctests prove a struct literal and a clone-and-overwrite do not compile — but `LinePart` has public fields, `ProjectionParts` has public fields, and `PlayableProjection::from_parts` is public. A downstream crate fabricates a line by writing a `LinePart` literal and calling `from_parts`

THE PROOF IS CHECKED IN AND WAS WRITTEN TO PROVE SOMETHING ELSE: `parts_are_constructible_from_a_downstream_crate` constructs a `LinePart` with arbitrary text from outside the kernel and ingests it. It exists to show the parts type carries no crate-private member; it also shows the door

DECISION: give prose the SAME seam the projection has — `PassagePart` / `PassagesParts` / `to_part` / `passages_from_parts`, and `emit_passages` in the Round 786 shape (`OnceLock`, body-scoped `CELL`, chunked bodies, the shared `artifact` assembler). A different, stronger contract for prose would be two answers to one question, and it would be fiction: the door is equally open either way and only the prose doc would claim otherwise

REJECTED, and recorded so they are not re-proposed. Closing the line door too deletes the build-time bake, which is the whole Round 764 to Round 786 arc. A `&'static`-only ingestion door — so fabricated prose must be a literal in the consumer's own source and cannot be driven by parsed data — is the only alternative that buys anything real, and it is still rejected: `Box::leak` defeats it, it forks the contract from the line axis, and Round 785 already rejected the type split a `&'static`-only kernel type forces. Reopen only if a consumer is MEASURED to need it

THREE DOCS MUST CHANGE IN THE SAME ROUND AS THE BUILD, because a half-done honesty fix is worse than none. `prose.rs`'s "invention is unrepresentable, for prose" becomes false and must say what is true: unrepresentable through the READING API, with the bake seam a deliberate named ingestion point. `Passage`'s two `compile_fail` doctests stay, with a line saying what they do NOT cover. And `ProjectionParts`' claim that `from_parts` needs no `Result` because "there is no untrusted input left to check it against" — true of emitted parts, false of typed ones, and the sentence is why this went unnoticed
verification_bullets: DESIGN round: no code changed, so no test claim is made. `validate-workspace` before and after: T1 orphan total=0, T3 reject=0, atomic orphan_refs 10+0 unchanged

The guard claim is verified against the code rather than argued: `Line::from_part` is `pub(crate)` and `Passage::from_excerpt` is `pub(crate)`, but `PlayableProjection::from_parts` is `pub` at `projection.rs`, `LinePart`'s fields are `pub` at `types.rs`, and `ProjectionParts`' are `pub`. The composition of those four visibilities is the door, and no single one of them looks like it

The borrowing question is deliberately NOT decided here, and the reason is that the number behind it is arithmetic rather than a measurement. Round 789 measured all three fields borrowed; text is roughly 99% of the fixture's bytes by construction (2,655 Korean characters against a ~20-byte source and a ~28-byte prefix), so borrowing TEXT ALONE should capture nearly all of the 97% while leaving `ContentAnchor` untouched. Untouched matters: `ContentAnchor` and `Locator` live in `mnemosyne-core` with serde derives and `String` fields, shared with the store

So the sequencing puts a MEASUREMENT between the two builds rather than after them: emit with owned text first (which is the consumer's whole ask, since the parse is what costs and not the copy), then measure the text-only arm, then borrow if it lands where the arithmetic says

The first consumer's third lift request asks the kernel to bake its passages, and Round 789 removed two of the three things that could have decided the shape: compile cost is 0.05s for the whole artifact, and the 319 KB longest line is flat in store size because `CHUNK` bounds ITEMS, so the Round 775 gate already passes. One question was left and it is the forgery guard

THE GUARD, STATED CORRECTLY: the kernel cannot give generated code a privilege the consumer lacks. Generated source is spliced into the CONSUMER's crate, so anything it calls, a hand-written line in that crate calls. Any bake door is a fabrication door, and no sealed token, checksum or `#[doc(hidden)]` changes that — they narrow discoverability, not capability

AND THAT TRADE WAS ALREADY MADE, ON THE LINE AXIS, WITHOUT BEING WRITTEN DOWN. `Line`'s fields are crate-private and two `compile_fail` doctests prove a struct literal and a clone-and-overwrite do not compile — but `LinePart` has public fields, `ProjectionParts` has public fields, and `PlayableProjection::from_parts` is public. A downstream crate fabricates a line by writing a `LinePart` literal and calling `from_parts`

THE PROOF IS CHECKED IN AND WAS WRITTEN TO PROVE SOMETHING ELSE: `parts_are_constructible_from_a_downstream_crate` constructs a `LinePart` with arbitrary text from outside the kernel and ingests it. It exists to show the parts type carries no crate-private member; it also shows the door

DECISION: give prose the SAME seam the projection has — `PassagePart` / `PassagesParts` / `to_part` / `passages_from_parts`, and `emit_passages` in the Round 786 shape (`OnceLock`, body-scoped `CELL`, chunked bodies, the shared `artifact` assembler). A different, stronger contract for prose would be two answers to one question, and it would be fiction: the door is equally open either way and only the prose doc would claim otherwise

REJECTED, and recorded so they are not re-proposed. Closing the line door too deletes the build-time bake, which is the whole Round 764 to Round 786 arc. A `&'static`-only ingestion door — so fabricated prose must be a literal in the consumer's own source and cannot be driven by parsed data — is the only alternative that buys anything real, and it is still rejected: `Box::leak` defeats it, it forks the contract from the line axis, and Round 785 already rejected the type split a `&'static`-only kernel type forces. Reopen only if a consumer is MEASURED to need it

THREE DOCS MUST CHANGE IN THE SAME ROUND AS THE BUILD, because a half-done honesty fix is worse than none. `prose.rs`'s "invention is unrepresentable, for prose" becomes false and must say what is true: unrepresentable through the READING API, with the bake seam a deliberate named ingestion point. `Passage`'s two `compile_fail` doctests stay, with a line saying what they do NOT cover. And `ProjectionParts`' claim that `from_parts` needs no `Result` because "there is no untrusted input left to check it against" — true of emitted parts, false of typed ones, and the sentence is why this went unnoticed
publishable_verification_bullets: DESIGN round: no code changed, so no test claim is made. `validate-workspace` before and after: T1 orphan total=0, T3 reject=0, atomic orphan_refs 10+0 unchanged

The guard claim is verified against the code rather than argued: `Line::from_part` is `pub(crate)` and `Passage::from_excerpt` is `pub(crate)`, but `PlayableProjection::from_parts` is `pub` at `projection.rs`, `LinePart`'s fields are `pub` at `types.rs`, and `ProjectionParts`' are `pub`. The composition of those four visibilities is the door, and no single one of them looks like it

The borrowing question is deliberately NOT decided here, and the reason is that the number behind it is arithmetic rather than a measurement. Round 789 measured all three fields borrowed; text is roughly 99% of the fixture's bytes by construction (2,655 Korean characters against a ~20-byte source and a ~28-byte prefix), so borrowing TEXT ALONE should capture nearly all of the 97% while leaving `ContentAnchor` untouched. Untouched matters: `ContentAnchor` and `Locator` live in `mnemosyne-core` with serde derives and `String` fields, shared with the store

So the sequencing puts a MEASUREMENT between the two builds rather than after them: emit with owned text first (which is the consumer's whole ask, since the parse is what costs and not the copy), then measure the text-only arm, then borrow if it lands where the arithmetic says
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: NEXT IS THE BUILD, and it carries the three doc corrections with it. Emitting without them would ship a kernel whose prose module says invention is unrepresentable while the same round makes it representable
The third arm of `prose_fixtures` — text borrowed, anchor owned — is not built. It is step 2 of the sequencing and the thing that turns §5's arithmetic into a figure
Step 1 changes nothing the consumer already calls, so unlike Round 786 it is not breaking for them; they gain an entry point. Whether they adopt it before or after validating it is theirs to sequence

The prose fixture is synthetic — one repeated sentence truncated to the mean length, not the consumer's 56 actual passages — so it prices bytes and item counts faithfully and says nothing about text that varies in ways rustc might charge for differently
What baking prose adds to their 2.68 MB baked projection is still unmeasured and depends on the shape chosen here

verification_bullets: MEASURED at 56 spots then 224, in-test with the thread-local counting allocator, beside the two arms already there: owned 171 then 680 allocations and 363,752 then 1,476,732 bytes; TEXT-ONLY 115 then 456 allocations and 12,560 then 69,564 bytes; fully borrowed 3 then 8 and 7,488 then 44,352

THE ARITHMETIC HELD ON THE AXIS IT WAS STATED ON. Borrowing the text alone keeps 98.2% of the byte win — 1,476,732 down to 69,564 against a full borrow's 44,352. On bytes the anchor really is the cheap half, and `mnemosyne-core` does not have to move for it

AND IT DOES NOT HOLD ON THE OTHER AXIS, WHICH IS THE ONE THE CONSUMER ORIGINALLY COMPLAINED ABOUT. On allocation CALLS the text-only arm keeps only a third of the win — 680 to 456, against a full borrow's 8 — because the anchor is two owned strings per spot and there is nothing else left. The first consumer's third field report was about call traffic, 43% of instructions in malloc and free, not about bytes

So the number Round 790 reasoned to was right and the sentence around it was not: "borrowing text alone captures nearly all of the 97%" is true of bytes and false of calls, and only measuring the arm separates them

What that means for the shape decision, stated as what the numbers support rather than as the decision itself: at the consumer's scale all three arms are noise against the 38,913 allocations Round 791 already removed by ending the parse, so the remaining choice is about the property rather than the cost — and moving the anchor means changing a `mnemosyne-core` type the store shares, for a saving nobody has measured a need for

changes_bullets: BUILD, step 3 of the Round 790 sequencing, and it names the property before it picks the arm — which is what Round 792 asked whoever took this to do. This round buys the BYTES and does not buy the calls

`Passage::text` becomes `Cow<'static, str>`, an implementation detail: the accessor still returns `&str`, so no caller sees it. A baked passage POINTS at the literal in the binary; `resolve` and `from_excerpt` keep owning, because they build their text at run time. One type with two ownership modes rather than two types — the Round 785 decision on the projection axis, reached again here for the same reason, that a split is permanent API surface for every consumer

THE ANCHOR STAYS OWNED, and that is the decision rather than an omission. Round 792 measured that the remaining allocation CALLS are the anchor's two owned strings per spot, and taking them means changing `ContentAnchor` in `mnemosyne-core`, where it carries serde derives and is shared with the store. No consumer has been measured to need it — the same reopen condition Round 785 set for its own step 3

`PassagePart::text` moves with it, so the emitter can write `Cow::Borrowed` of a literal. `to_part` on a live passage yields `Cow::Owned`, and the two compare equal by CONTENT, which is what keeps the live-to-baked round trip an equality rather than a shape check

A SECOND EMITTER PRIMITIVE, `str_literal`, because the existing `string` appends `.to_string()` to every literal it writes — which is the method call Round 782 measured as most of the 5.5x compile gap between an owned and a borrowed artifact. It is a separate function rather than a flag, since the two produce different TYPES and a boolean deciding a type at a call site reads correct while being wrong

AND THE BORROW IS PROVEN BY THE GAP RATHER THAN BY THE TYPE: the baked set CARRIES 348,371 bytes of prose while allocating 28,325. The text is not in that number. What is, is the map and the 168 owned anchor strings — exactly the residual Round 792 predicted and this round declined to take
`baked == live` again on the real store, text and anchor, across all 56 passages, with the store read and never written

THE GATE IS THE DISCRIMINANT, NOT THE CONTENT, and it had to be. `Cow` compares by content, so the round trip, the live-to-baked equality and the emitter's own fixture all pass identically whether the baked passage points at the literal or copied it. `the_ingestion_door_carries_the_borrow_it_was_given` asserts the variant, in both directions: a borrowed part must stay borrowed and an owned one must stay owned

changes_bullets: BUILD, step 2 of the Round 785 ladder, on the axis Round 794 priced. `Line` and `LinePart` now hold `Cow<'static, str>` for every string and `Cow<'static, [Cow<'static, str>]>` for the entity list. A BAKED line points at the literals in the binary; `Line::from_disclosed` keeps owning, because it derives its strings from a store read at run time. One type with two ownership modes rather than two types - the Round 785 decision, reached again here for the same reason it was reached for prose in Round 793

THE LIST IS A `Cow` AND NOT A `Vec<Cow<..>>`, which is the decision Round 785 deferred to this round and Round 794 settled: a `Vec` spine costs one allocation per line whatever the strings do, so stopping there is 80% of the win rather than 100%. The emitter writes the slice INLINE and relies on rvalue static promotion, verified by compilation together with its discriminating half rather than assumed, because a named `static` per line would add an item per line and Round 789 measured that rustc charges per item

THE ACCESSOR IS AN ITERATOR, `entities(&self) -> impl ExactSizeIterator<Item = &str>`, and this is the one form Round 785 left open on the grounds that it needs the call sites. With them in hand there is exactly ONE caller outside this crate, so ergonomics did not decide it - the design's own commitment did. `Cow` is meant to stay an implementation detail, and `&[Cow<'static, str>]` would publish it in the signature of the most-read accessor on the most-read type. The iterator hides it, hides it for BOTH holdings (Round 794 verified by compilation that a `Vec<Cow<..>>` and a `Cow<'static, [Cow<..>]>` yield the identical `&str` sequence, so the signature does not pin the field either), and keeps Round 786's property, since a `&'static self` yields `&'static str` items by the same elision that made the handle work

SCOPE IS THE LINE AXIS AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. `CastPart`, `ForkPart`, `DoorPart`, `Rung`, `ChoiceEntityRef` and the quest parts still own. `Line` is the shape Round 794 measured, and it is where the count is: the first consumer holds 4,612 lines against tens of everything else, so the line axis is the overwhelming majority of the per-startup allocations the whole ladder exists to remove. Extending the same holding to the rest is mechanical and is the next round, not a carry hidden in this one

Round 799 — a separator is interior or i.decision_summary: R799 (FIX, MNEMO-GAP-002) — the `§<id>` extractor swallowed a separating slash into the preceding id, so `§1/§3` parsed as `1/` and `3` and the gate reported SectionMissing — the hallucination class — against a comment citing two real sections. The reporter's recommended repair was to close the id charset to numerics, which was declined: slash slugs are a documented, tested id shape and this very store holds `code-citation-defense/bidirectional-binding`, so that repair would have traded one false hallucination verdict for another. The rule landed instead is the one the grammar already applied to `.`: a separator belongs to the id only when it is INTERIOR, flanked by id characters on both sides. A slug never starts or ends with its separator and a slash between two cites never has one on the far side, so the cases separate without a delimiter list to maintain. `§1/x` stays one id, which is the honest limit — with an id char on both sides the slash is interior, and no token can tell a two-segment slug from a pair whose second cite lost its sigil.

Round 801 — the list joiner the ASCII se.decision_summary: R801 (BUILD) — the chain rule let an external prefix carry across `/` and whitespace only, so Korean prose enumerating with the middle dot (`첫날 §4·§6·§7·§13`) named one document four times and drew three SectionMissing hallucination verdicts; five of the reporting workspace's fifteen residual violations were this one character. `·` and `・` now chain and `、` deliberately does not, matching the comma rule Round 380 already stated. Unlike Round 800 this set is SEMANTIC and cannot derive its oracle from the charset — nothing about `/` or `.` says which joins and which ends a sentence — so it stays a closed list and the test states the contrast, a joining column and a breaking column. The two failure directions are not symmetric: a character missing from the joining set costs a visible false positive, while a character wrongly reaching it turns the axis off for every cite behind it and nothing reports that, which is also why the set is not workspace-configurable. `-` was declined despite Round 800 adding it to the id charset, because a spaced hyphen is a dash and the reporter's corpus holds zero hyphen chains.
changes_bullets: BUILD, from the same downstream field report Round 799 answered. The chain rule (Round 380 path (c)) let a cite inherit an external prefix across `/` and whitespace only. Korean prose enumerates with the middle dot, so `첫날 §4·§6·§7·§13` named one document four times and the gate returned three `SectionMissing` — the hallucination class — against a correct citation. Five of the reporter's fifteen residual violations were this one character

`·` (U+00B7) AND `・` (U+30FB) NOW CHAIN, and `、` (U+3001) deliberately does not. The middle dot is the Korean and Japanese list joiner and plays the exact role `/` plays in `UAX #9 §6.6.8 / §6.6.9`; the ideographic comma is a comma, so it breaks, which is the rule Round 380 already stated for `,` rather than a new one

THE SET IS SEMANTIC AND CANNOT DERIVE ITS ORACLE, which is the one thing that separates it from Round 800. That round could ask the charset which characters are separators, because "no id begins or ends with one" is structurally true of every separator. Here nothing about `/` or `.` says which joins and which ends a sentence. So the set stays a closed hand list and the test states the CONTRAST — a joining column and a breaking column — since a rule with no derivable oracle has to pin both sides or it pins neither

THE TWO FAILURE DIRECTIONS ARE NOT SYMMETRIC, and that is why the breaking column exists. A character missing from the joining set costs a false positive, which is visible and gets reported. A character wrongly reaching it turns the axis OFF for every cite behind it and nothing reports that. The set is therefore deliberately NOT workspace-configurable: a workspace could otherwise list `.` and never see a violation again

`-` WAS DECLINED, though Round 800 added it to the id charset. A spaced hyphen is a dash — `RFC 2131 §3 - our §5-4` is two documents, not two sections of one — so chaining it would stop checking the cite after every dash in a comment. The reporter's corpus holds five `·` chains and zero `-` chains. This is a decision with a resumption condition, a measured instance, not an omission

Round 804 — the gate that was weighing a.decision_summary: R804 (BUILD) — the Round 798 design landed as written: eleven projection fields and their `ProjectionParts` mirror moved to `Cow<'static, str>`, `walk`/`spine` became iterators over a crate-private `walk_raw`, and the discriminant gate asserts the variant on a KEY as well as a value because 938 of the 1,316 moved strings are keys and a door that rebuilt only its keys would pass any value-only assertion. On this crate's own 800-line fixture the shipped emitter now writes 0 owned constructions against 5 before — exactly the residual Round 795 named. What the design did not predict is that the stack gate would go red on the QUEST ratio while nothing in the quest axis had changed: the emitted quest source was byte-identical and every compiled frame in it was identical, checked by disassembling both binaries and diffing the frame table. The cause was the probe's own dispatcher, six fixtures as six arms of one `match`, which at opt-level 0 is one frame holding every arm's temporaries — so the figure reported for any fixture carried what the others wanted. Split into one `#[inline(never)]` function per fixture, quest returns to 8 KiB flat, playable stays 32 KiB flat, and the control still grows 86 KiB to 303 KiB, so the arm that licenses the others still discriminates. The consumer's real-store allocation delta is NOT measured: their checkout was being written to while this ran, and the cross-repo rule is read-only at most against an occupied tree.
changes_bullets: BUILD of the Round 798 design, in one round because the fields are one struct and its `to_parts` mirror, and a half-moved projection is a struct carrying two conventions. Eleven fields moved to `Cow<'static, str>` — `telling`, `by_world`'s two key levels, `walks` and its elements, `titles` key and value, `cast` and `ask_doors` section keys, `divergent_endings`, and `journal_offers` to its leaves — with `Interactivity`, `Door`'s payload and `Fork` left owned on the Round 796 boundary

`walk` AND `spine` ARE NOW ITERATORS over a crate-private `walk_raw`, which is the accessor question open since Round 785. The two in-crate indexing callers read the resolver; the gate's two walk loops call the accessor twice rather than holding a slice, because an iterator is consumed once and two hash lookups are not worth publishing the representation in the signature of the most-read accessor

A NEW `JournalOffers` ALIAS on the live side, for the reason `SectionLines` was named in Round 769 rather than for tidiness: expanded, the type is four levels deep and `clippy::type_complexity` rejects it under the `-D warnings` this workspace runs and a consumer is entitled to run

THE GATE ASSERTS THE DISCRIMINANT ON A KEY, which is what the design said it had to. Round 798 attributed 938 of the 1,316 moved strings to map keys, so a door that rebuilt only its keys would pass any assertion written over values. `the_projection_door_carries_the_borrow_on_its_keys_too` walks a labelled enumeration of every moved scalar in a projection and asserts the variant in both directions; the live half is `the_runtime_projection_constructor_still_owns`

THE FIXTURE'S NON-VACUITY IS ASSERTED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. The walk is checked to reach thirteen scalars before anything is asserted about them, because a fixture that stopped populating a field would silently shrink the loop and every assertion under it would still pass

A FALSE DOCTEST WAS FOUND FAILING FOR THE WRONG REASON, the Round 795 discipline applied again: the `compile_fail` pair proving the baked accessor hands out `'static` was failing on the fixture's own type error, not on the lifetime it exists to prove.
