Round 838.decision_summary:
R838 (DESIGN — the ref ids become types, because the cheaper answer was chosen under a frame the owner had already overturned). Round 834 deferred newtyping the ref ids as "structurally the right answer but it touches every ref field and its callers to close one defect", and picked a source tripwire plus a hand classification instead. That parenthetical is a COST argument, and Round 824 established the standing instruction that cost is not the deciding factor. Asked directly whether the built answer was the most long-term-correct one, it is not. This designs the migration to types.

WHAT THE TABLE CANNOT DO, from its own entry: it catches an UNCLASSIFIED place and never a MISCLASSIFIED one, its parser is a line-based reading of Rust rather than a parse, and it is ninety-four lines of artifact maintained beside the types it describes. A type says the same thing in the one place that cannot drift from the value. It also buys something the table can never see: a detector that checks a ref against the WRONG registry is a compile error, where today nothing would notice.

ROUND 837 WAS NOT WASTE AND IS THE PRECONDITION. Round 834 said the table would become the work list for exactly this, and it did — but more than that, filling it is what found the five coverage paths, the seven places with no re-check, and the fact that continuity checks live behind a different command. Starting the migration without that map would have meant touching forty-three ref fields blind.

"SCHEMA 0" IS MEASURED, NOT ASSERTED, on a scratch crate outside the repo. A `#[serde(transparent)]` newtype over String is byte-identical to a bare String in FIELD position and in MAP-KEY position, deserializes as a key, keeps `contains_key("literal")` working through `Borrow<str>`, sorts identically to String, and emits the same JSON Schema in field position with or without `#[schemars(transparent)]`. The map-key result is the one that matters: the registries keyed by id are where a type turns "which registry is this a key of" into something the compiler holds. The ordering result is the one that would have been expensive to miss — a different Ord moves BTreeMap iteration and every deterministic-order claim in the codebase with it.

THE MEASUREMENT ALSO CAUGHT ME COMPARING THE WRONG THING. The first schema comparison included the schema `title`, which differs by fixture name, and reported the newtype as changing the schema. Comparing the `properties` subtree — the part a consumer reads — shows it identical. That is the third time this session a conclusion from a quick reading did not survive being checked properly.

THE COST IS 763 CALL SITES across nine registries, and it is stated rather than softened: sections 225, narrative_facts 152, branches 109, entities 104, frames 72, entity_kinds 52, predicates 38, units 6, parameters 5.

`Borrow<str>` IS ADOPTED, DECIDED BY MEASUREMENT: of 132 `contains_key` calls, 53 pass a literal, and without `Borrow` every one becomes a constructor call that adds noise without adding safety. What this concedes must be said plainly — the safety a newtype buys is in ASSIGNMENT and FIELD position, not in lookup. `fact.frame = entity_id` becomes a compile error; `entities.contains_key(frame.as_str())` does not. Closing lookup too is a typed accessor per registry, not the removal of `Borrow`, and it is follow-on work.

ORDER: smallest first, one or two registries per round, each round compiling and green — `UnitId` + `ParameterId` (11 sites) proves the recipe end-to-end including a map-key change, then ascending to `SectionId` (225) last. Every round verifies store JSON byte-identity against real stores, moves its rows in the Round 837 table, and injects a cross-registry assignment that must fail to compile — the class the table can never catch.

WHAT THIS DELIBERATELY DOES NOT BUY, so the next round does not overclaim: lookup safety (above); WHICH gate covers a field, which stays a hand classification of the five paths; and the seven `WritePathOnly` places, where a type makes it obvious where a check belongs without writing one. And going further than newtypes is WORSE, not better: enforcing registry membership at construction would make a corrupted store fail at LOAD, when `validate-workspace`'s whole job is to enumerate violations rather than die on the first, and would make the phase-2 forward ref structurally impossible.

Round 838 designed the migration from `String` ids to nine typed ones and ordered it smallest-first so the recipe is established where a mistake is cheap. This is `UnitId` and `ParameterId`: the two smallest registries, five and six call sites, carrying every shape the larger ones will hit — a struct field, an enum struct-variant field, two map keys, a nested map key, and a generic helper written against `BTreeMap<String, T>`.

THE PROOF IS THE INJECTION THE OLD GUARD COULD NEVER RUN. Round 837's table catches an unclassified field; it cannot catch a check that resolves a ref against the WRONG registry, because to a `String` every registry looks alike. Two injections now fail to COMPILE: assigning a `ParameterId` into `EdgeCost.unit`, and — the one that matters — `store.units.contains_key(&gate.parameter)`, a detector looking a parameter up in the units registry. THE CONCEDED LIMIT WAS INJECTED TOO, rather than only written down. `store.units.contains_key(gate.parameter.as_str())` still compiles, exactly as Round 838 said it would: `Borrow<str>` is kept because 53 of 132 `contains_key` calls pass a literal, and the safety a newtype buys is in assignment and field position rather than in lookup. Round 840.decision_summary:
R840 (BUILD — an exclusion is a claim, and nothing checked it; plus the two message defects and the pin-floor correction the field report raised). The external spec consumer adopted Round 835 in order, reported all five workspaces green, and sent back four observations. One of them indicts advice this project gave: our reply told them to silence the remaining scan-coverage failure with four exclusion globs, they checked the trees BY HAND before declaring them, and found 55 hand-authored citations those exclusions would have silently un-gated. The advice produced exit 0 and would have cost real coverage. Nothing in the tool could tell the difference.

`scan_exclusions` ASSERTS "no citation this ledger gates lives here" and nothing verified the assertion. This adds the verification, and it is the vacuity Round 783 already refuses seen one level up: that round made a configured-but-EMPTY scan set loud, and this makes a scan set emptied BY DECLARATION loud.

THE AXIS IS "ONLY", NOT "ANY", and that distinction is the whole design. The same consumer's other exclusions are honest and must stay silent: their codegen output cites the same section ids as the templates that generate it, the templates stay scanned, so excluding the output re-checks one string twice. A detector firing on any citation inside an excluded tree would reject that and teach people to stop declaring exclusions at all. So a citation also present in a scanned file loses nothing, and a citation present only in excluded trees is gone — set difference.

THE FIRST VERSION WAS WRONG AND THE CONSUMER'S OWN STORE SHOWED IT. Run against their WIRE ledger it reported fifteen swallowed citations on a CORRECTLY configured workspace: `§10.2`-shaped SCXML citations that the SCXML ledger gates and the wire ledger never could. Their report said "no citation of this namespace lives here" and I had dropped the namespace. Scoping to the ledger's own section set takes it to zero on their fixed config and to exactly four — `wire-W1`, `W3`, `W4`, `W5` — on the pre-fix config that excluded `sce-build/` instead of scanning it. Those four are what they found by hand.

TWO INJECTIONS REPORTED ZERO AND BOTH WERE RIGHT TO BE SUSPECTED. Disabling `comment_only` changed nothing because every citation in the fixture sat in a comment; adding a citation-shaped token in CODE made that axis load-bearing. Removing the namespace scoping changed nothing because every cited id was already in the fixture's store; adding a citation of a section the store does NOT hold made that one load-bearing too. A zero-finding injection is a statement about the fixture, not about the guard.

THE OTHER TWO ITEMS, both theirs, both real. The refusal message stated the pin twice — "pins `X`, and this build is `Y`, and the workspace pins `X`" — because `PinRefusal::Different`'s Display restated what its one caller had already opened with. The pin is dropped from that variant only; the other three do not overlap the opener. And a stamp is `--abbrev=8` while a pin is legal at seven characters, so the two printed side by side can differ in width and never be string-equal even when they match; the message now states that the comparison is by prefix rather than truncating the stamp, which would misreport what the build is.

THE PIN FLOOR IS NOT ROUND 826. Field-tested: their pre-`[tool]` binary never reached the pin because it died on `scan_exclusions`, a key from an EARLIER round sitting further up the same config. Round 828 called the circularity semantically specific to `[tool]` while noting the mechanism was general; the consumer's observation joins those correctly — any key newer than the running binary poisons parsing first, so a pin guards only against revisions newer than the newest key beside it, and nothing inside a config can guard against an older binary. The `--version` assertion in the shell recipe covers that direction, which is why that recipe is not superseded by `[tool]`.

Round 841.decision_summary:
R841 (BUILD — `PredicateId`, the third registry id, and the first one whose ref reaches every layer). Migration 2 of 8 in the Round 838 arc. Round 842.decision_summary:
R842 (BUILD — `EntityKindId`, the first id that four fields across three registries were already sharing without saying so). Migration 3 of 8. `Entity::kind`, `EntityKind::parents`, `Predicate::subject_kind` and `Predicate::object_entity_kind` all hold entity-kind vocabulary, and until today nothing in any of their types said they were the same vocabulary. That is the shape the recipe had not met: the previous two rounds each typed ONE field plus a map key.

THE ROUND'S REAL WORK WAS TWO HELPERS, NOT THE FIELDS. `entity_kind()` returned `Option<&str>` and `is_kind_or_subkind()` took `&str`, so the obvious migration — convert with `.as_str()` at each call — would have typed the fields and then thrown the type away one line later, at the exact place the reachability question is asked. Both are now typed end to end, which is what makes the injections below fail rather than compile.

TWO INJECTIONS, BOTH COMPILE ERRORS: an entity's KIND looked up in the ENTITIES registry (the two maps this file touches most, one line apart), and a `PredicateId` assigned into `Predicate::subject_kind`. The second is the one this round exists for — `Predicate` carries both a predicate id and two entity-kind ids, and before today they were the same type.

THE MACRO GREW `is_empty`, AND THE REASON MATTERS. `Entity::kind` spells "unset" as the empty string and skips it on the wire with `skip_serializing_if = "String::is_empty"`. Without an `is_empty` on the id the attribute breaks, and the path of least resistance would have been to leave that ONE field a `String` — reopening exactly the hole this migration closes, in the field with 167 live values. One method in the shared macro instead.

SELF-REPORT: I DAMAGED UNRELATED CODE WITH AN OVER-BROAD REGEX. A pattern meant to retype `Some("x"), "y"` in two test calls also rewrote five `assert_eq!` message arguments elsewhere in the file, which surfaced as `format argument must be a string literal`. Recovered by diffing against HEAD and restoring each line, then finishing the work with per-line edits driven by the compiler's own error positions. The project rule about regex risking file damage exists for this; I ran the risk and paid it. The remaining passes asked `cargo` for the exact lines and touched only those.

MEASURED ON REAL DATA WITH ONE AXIS ADMITTEDLY EMPTY. The consumer's store has 8 entity kinds and 167 entities, and ALL 167 carry a kind — that leg round-trips through the new types and compares identical. But `EntityKind::parents` holds ZERO entries in every store that exists, so the inheritance leg is covered by injection and unit tests only. Saying "real-data verified" without that sentence would be the empty-axis claim this project keeps catching.

R843 (BUILD — `FrameId`, and the name that was lying). Migration 4 of 8. The store holds a frame id in exactly two places, the `frames` registry key and `NarrativeFact::frame`, and typing those two was the small half of the round.

THE NAME SAID FRAME AND THE VALUE NEVER WAS ONE. `NarrativeFact::supersedes_in_frame` holds a FACT id. THE COMPILER CANNOT LIST THE REMAINING WORK, AND THAT IS NEW. `PartialEq<&str>` is on the shared macro by design, so a helper that kept `frame: &str` still compares clean against the now-typed field — it compiles, it is wrong, and nothing says so. `disclosure_leak` was exactly that: it took `truth_frame: &str`, compared it against 1106 typed fields, and never appeared in any error list. DIFFERENTIAL AGAINST A REAL PRIOR BINARY. Our own tests passing proves the tests still pass. So the pinned consumer binary from `5481f72e`, four rounds older than this change, ran the same queries over the same store: all 22 frame-view projections byte-identical, and the store after a real `add-frame` and a real `add-fact` byte-identical. Round 845.decision_summary:
R845 (BUILD — `BranchId`, and the algebra that turned out to be the round). Migration 6 of 8. Four places hold a branch id, which sounded like the small half — and then the world-line ALGEBRA turned out to be where a branch id actually lives.

THE FIELDS WERE FOUR; THE FUNCTIONS WERE THIRTY. `world_membership` and its memo, `forward_confluences`, `is_confluence`, `is_known_world`, `succession_branch_inherits`, `road_lineage`, `road_of`, `lineage_of`, `world_order_composition`, `visibility`, `WorldCtx`, and eight `CanonOrder` accessors all take or return a world-line, and every one of them would have kept compiling with `&str`. That is the Round 843 rule at full scale: `PartialEq<&str>` means the compiler cannot list this work, so it was found by reading the graph of who takes a world.

`query_worlds` HAD TO STOP BORROWING. It returned `Vec<&str>` because `MAIN_BRANCH` is a `&str` const — there is no registry entry to borrow an id from, main being known by construction and never registered. So it now returns owned ids, and the one function that knows main belongs in the world list is the one that constructs it.

TWO INJECTIONS, BOTH COMPILE ERRORS: a world resolved against the FRAMES registry, and a `FrameId` handed to `lineage_of`. Both live in `frame_view(store, order, frame, branch, ...)`, where a frame and a branch sit adjacent in the argument list and were the same type three rounds ago.

SELF-REPORT — A VACUOUS PARITY CHECK, CAUGHT. The first write-differential reported "byte-identical" while both binaries had REJECTED the command (wrong flag names) and written nothing: two untouched copies compare equal. The check that caught it was asserting the branch count actually rose. A parity test that cannot tell "both did the same thing" from "neither did anything" is the empty-axis claim in a new costume.

DIFFERENTIAL ACROSS EVERY WORLD-LINE THE CONSUMER DECLARES: 9 branches, 6 forks, 3 confluences, 662 of 1106 facts off `main`. The pinned `5481f72e` binary and this build agree byte for byte on 15 runs and ~9.7 MB, including a separate manuscript per branch — which is what actually exercises the fork/merge lattice rather than just loading it.

R846 (BUILD — `FactId`, and the field whose name has been lying since Round 434). Migration 7 of 8. Eight places hold a fact ref and five side tables are KEYED by one, which makes this the most connected registry in the store.

THE NAME. `NarrativeFact::supersedes_in_frame` holds a FACT id. Round 843 could not fix it — `FactId` did not exist yet — so it documented the lie on `FrameId` and left the field alone. Today the type says what the value is, and the injection proves the confusion was reachable: assigning a `FrameId` into `supersedes_in_frame` compiled without complaint yesterday and is a type error now.

FIVE SIDE TABLES WERE KEYED BY A FACT AND SAID SO ONLY IN PROSE. `edge_costs`, `edge_guards`, `parameter_deltas`, `parameter_gates` and `fact_counts` each carry a doc comment reading "keyed by the fact id"; none of them carried a type that did. They do now, so a side table cannot be keyed by a branch or a section by accident.

THE READ PATH WAS THE LARGER HALF AGAIN. `holds_at`, `successors_index`, `succession_ancestors`, the world-pair visitor's callback signature, `resolve_fact_disclosure` and `DisclosurePlan::effective` all took a fact id as `&str`, and every one of them would have kept compiling — the Round 843 rule holding for a third round: `PartialEq<&str>` means the compiler cannot enumerate this work.

TWO INJECTIONS, BOTH COMPILE ERRORS, both about the same confusion from opposite directions: a fact looked up in the frames registry, and a frame id stored in the fact-ref field named after frames.

DIFFERENTIAL: ten reports over the consumer's 1106 facts — including irony intervals and payoff substantiation, which walk the conflict and succession graphs this round retyped — byte-identical against the pinned `5481f72e` binary, plus a byte-identical store after a real `add-fact`. Two legs are honestly empty everywhere (`TypedObject::Fact` objects and `fact_counts`) and are named as injection-only in the verification.

FOUR fact-keyed side tables typed with it — `edge_costs`, `edge_guards`, `parameter_deltas`, `parameter_gates`, plus `fact_counts` — so a side table can no longer be keyed by anything but the fact it hangs on

Round 848.decision_summary:
R848 (DESIGN — lookup safety: the measurement Round 838 made is stale, and it decided the other way). Round 838 kept `Borrow<str>` on the ref ids and wrote the reason down honestly: 132 `contains_key` calls, 53 of them string literals, so removing the impl "converts every one into a constructor call that adds noise without adding safety". That was measured BEFORE the migration. Nine ids later it is worth re-measuring rather than inheriting.

WHAT THE REMOVAL ACTUALLY BREAKS, measured by deleting the impl and reading the compiler: 250 errors in the two crates the build reaches, 175 of them in test fixtures and 75 in source; downstream crates unmeasured because atomic fails first. What it does NOT break is the class Round 838 may have been picturing — the String-keyed report and count maps looked up with `id.as_str()` resolve through std's `String: Borrow<str>`, not ours, and are untouched. So the cost is narrower than the old measurement implies and lands almost entirely on fixture literals.

WHY THE ALTERNATIVE IS WORSE, also measured: privatising the registry maps behind typed accessors touches 489 field uses, 221 of which are test `insert` calls. Fixtures construct stores by inserting directly, so privatisation needs an `insert` accessor — and an `insert` accessor restores exactly the hole privatisation was meant to close. Bigger change, weaker guarantee.

WHAT THE REMOVAL BUYS, precisely: `entities.contains_key(unit.as_str())` — the example `ids.rs` has carried as a known hole since Round 838 — stops compiling, everywhere, including in tests. That is the wrong-REGISTRY class. It is not the wrong-VALUE class, and this entry does not claim it is.

A FIND WHILE MEASURING: two import paths (`import_ladders`, `import_epub_excerpts`) look a raw DTO `String` up in the sections registry and never construct a `SectionId` at all. Their existence checks run on untyped text today. The removal forces those conversions into view, which is the boundary discipline the whole arc has been applying everywhere else.

Round 851.decision_summary:
R851 (BUILD — the store gained 70 KB and the projection gained 91 MB, and the difference was one line copied 98 times). Lift request 6 from the playable consumer, and the narrowest they have sent: the emitted shape, with no new concept in the schema or the API.

THE DIAGNOSIS THEY BROUGHT WAS RIGHT AND THEY HAD ALREADY CORRECTED IT ONCE. Their build script said the same SCENE repeats per world-line; they reopened the artifact, found the prose appears zero times in it, and sent the corrected version — what repeats is the disclosed LINE. Round 791 had already taken the prose out of this axis and into `emit_passages`, and that decision held. The unclosed half was `LinePart`.

WHAT THE PROJECTION EMITS is `world -> section -> lines`, and a section walked by seven world-lines carried its disclosures seven times. On their store: 4,654 emitted lines over 882 distinct ones, and at 509 branches 86,754 over the SAME 882. The sidecar grew 71 KB for those 500 branches. The file grew with the cross product of scenes and worlds while the store grew with neither, so authoring paid for endings it had not written: 171 seconds and 4 GB of rustc, which on a smaller machine is not slow but OOM.

SO THE PAYLOAD IS EMITTED ONCE AND A WORLD-LINE NAMES IT BY POSITION. Their request wrote the pool keyed by `fact_id`, and that is true of every store measured — 882 ids over 882 payloads, no fact carrying two. It is not true of the TYPE. `mode` is a per-telling disclosure and nothing in the projection forbids one world stating what another hints, so a fact-id key would keep one of the two and lose the other silently. The pool is keyed by the RENDERED TEXT instead, which collapses exactly the lines that are the same line and cannot lose a difference because the rendered text carries every field. That is a correction to what was asked for, not a widening of it.

WHERE IT LIVES IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE ANSWER. The interning is entirely inside the generator: `ProjectionParts` is unchanged, `PlayableProjection` is unchanged, every accessor is unchanged, and the generated `build` reassembles the identical parts. The consumer changes no call site, which is what they asked and also what makes this reviewable — the live projection has no cross product to intern, so the kernel has no business learning about one. What moved is the one place that materialises it.

MEASURED ON THEIR STORE, READ-ONLY, ON BOTH SIDES OF THE CHANGE. Nine branches: 3.48 MB -> 0.81 MB, 3.66s -> 1.21s, 345 MB -> 230 MB. Five hundred and nine: 67.4 MB -> 6.57 MB, 171s -> 13.3s, 4.01 GB -> 1.06 GB. Startup did not pay: 1.54ms -> 1.41ms.

AND IT IS NOT FINISHED, WHICH IS WORTH SAYING PLAINLY. The RUNTIME still materialises the cross product — `from_parts` clones a pool entry per world-line — so the projection in memory is still worlds times lines. It measures harmless at this scale (36ms, 57.6 MB at 509 branches) and it is the residual: this round took the product out of the SOURCE, and closing it in memory would change `lines()` from a slice to a sequence, which is the consumer API break this request was careful not to be.
changes_bullets: `LinePool` in the generator interns every emitted line by its RENDERED TEXT and `by_world` emits `__mn_lines(__mn_pool, [positions])` — the payload once, the positions per world-line. This is the prescription Round 791 wrote for prose on the passage axis, applied to the axis that was still copying

The key is the rendered text and NOT the `fact_id` the request proposed: `LinePart::mode` is a per-telling disclosure and nothing forbids one world stating what another hints, so a fact-id key would silently keep one of two payloads — a half-enforced invariant rather than an invariant

`chunked_over` threads a `Param` through the three `by_world` nesting levels so the pool is a `build` local that dies with construction, rather than parked in a process-lifetime `OnceLock`. `chunked` is that with `None`, so there is one chunker and not two that could drift. The parameter is `_`-prefixed because a chunk of 50 may hold only worlds with no section, and an unread parameter breaks a consumer running `-D warnings`

NOTHING IN THE KERNEL MOVED — `ProjectionParts`, `PlayableProjection` and every accessor are untouched, `build` reassembles the identical parts, and the consumer changes no call site. Schema 0, API 0, generated-source shape only, which is exactly what the request asked for

The crate's own fixture gained a SECOND world-line through the same scene: the same two disclosures in the opposite order, its `f-a` differing from `main`'s in `mode` alone. One world could not have caught any of the three failure modes

INJECTION 2 — DROP THE PER-WORLD ORDER (sort the positions): two tests fail on the fixture, AND the real-store differential fails with "the pooled artifact rebuilt a different projection". The oracle discriminates on real data, not only on a hand fixture

INJECTION 3 — DISABLE INTERNING (never reuse a position): EVERY round-trip test stays green and only `a_disclosure_many_worlds_walk_is_emitted_once` fails, at 2,000 constructors against 100. That is the whole reason the collapse gate exists — a generator that copies is CORRECT, just not what this round is

Equal over 7 worlds and 4,654 lines, with the line count and the world count asserted in the test so an empty projection cannot pass

Round 852.decision_summary:
R852 (DEBT — Round 851 introduced this generator's first hash map, and the crate's oldest promise is that an unchanged store emits a byte-identical file). Found by re-reading Round 851 rather than by anything failing, which is the only way this one could have been found: it does not fail.

WHAT THE HAZARD IS. `LinePool` holds a `Vec` for the emission order and a `HashMap` for the lookup, and that separation is what keeps the artifact stable. `HashMap` iteration is SEEDED PER PROCESS. A later round that emits the pool from the map — the obvious simplification, since the map already holds every distinct line — produces an artifact that is completely correct and whose bytes differ on every build. Measured with exactly that change in place: three renders of one unchanged consumer store in three processes gave three different sha256s, and eleven of twelve tests stayed green, including the real-store differential against the previous generator.

WHY IT LANDS ON THE CONSUMER'S FRESHEST FIX. Their lift request 6 closed with a defect they claimed as their own: `build-store.sh` rewrites the sidecar, cargo watches mtime, and an unchanged store rebuilt anyway. They shipped the fix the same day by hashing the file's CONTENT. A generator that emitted different bytes for the same store would defeat that fix in a way that reads as their bug — the store is unchanged, the hash differs, so the hash must be wrong.

THE GATE ASSERTS THE SEPARATION FROM OUTSIDE. Three world-lines whose distinct ids are neither sorted nor reverse-sorted in first-seen order, and the emitted pool must match the walk. That refuses a `BTreeMap` reached for as readily as a `HashMap`: what is gated is that the order comes from `rendered`, not that it happens to be reproducible.

THE HONEST SHAPE OF THIS ROUND. Nothing was broken and nothing is fixed. What changed is that the invariant Round 851 depended on is now enforced instead of merely observed, and the doc on the field says which of the two structures owns the order. This is the class of defect the tests cannot find, so the tests had to be told about it.

The fixture defeats a `BTreeMap` reached for as well as a `HashMap`: any emission order that is not `LinePool::rendered`'s fails, not merely the seeded one

`LinePool::positions` is documented as a LOOKUP INDEX that nothing may iterate, naming the gate that holds it from outside. `rendered` is documented as the emission order and the only thing that decides it

Round 853.decision_summary:
R853 (DESIGN — the owner asked whether Round 851 chose the correct method with cost ignored, and two of the three answers are self-corrections). The question is the one that produced Round 838, and it earns the same kind of answer: the decision was right, one stated reason was wrong, and one deferral was a cost judgment wearing a scope judgment's clothes.

CORRECTION ONE — THE POOL KEY IS RIGHT AND ITS STATED REASON IS NOT. Round 851 refused the consumer's fact-id key because "`mode` is a per-telling disclosure and nothing forbids one world stating what another hints". A `MapLocator` resolves `mode` and `object` per (telling, fact); a projection carries exactly one telling; a world decides only WHICH facts it sees, never how they surface. So a fact cannot carry two payloads, the 882-of-882 measurement is a consequence rather than luck, and the fact-id key WOULD have been correct against today's upstream. The decision survives on a reason Round 851 did not give: the rendered-text key is LOCALLY exact, while the fact-id key would make this generator depend on a property of a type in another crate that nothing at this boundary can check and one added field would break silently. Both keys pool to the same 882, so the general one is free.

CORRECTION TWO — THE DEFERRAL WAS A COST JUDGMENT. Round 851's carry said the runtime cross product is "NOT closed" and that closing it "changes `lines()` from a slice to a sequence and is a consumer API break". Three things are wrong with that sentence. It makes the consumer's request scope the arbiter of what is correct. It calls a materialised read model an unclosed defect, when materialising answers is what a read model is for. And the alternative it names does not even work: positions inside the projection shrink each entry roughly fiftyfold and leave the cross product exactly where it was.

WHAT THE REAL ALTERNATIVE IS, AND THAT IT COSTS NO API. The store's Round 438 shared history means a fork child INHERITS its ancestor's facts up to the fork point, so a child's pre-fork spots are derived rather than authored. A projection can therefore store a spot only where it DIFFERS from what its fork parent answers, and `lines(world, section)` walks up the chain to the owner — returning that world's `&[Line]`, so the API break named as the blocker does not exist. Measured exact: 0 disagreements over 6,607 pre-fork comparisons across three stores, against 84 to 26,484 spots that do differ after the fork. It would store 1,238 lines against 4,654 on the consumer's real store.

AND WHY IT IS NOT BUILT. The cost lands on the read path of a running game: lookup depth 20, mean 7.29, on a twenty-deep chain against one hash lookup today. The consumer's design is a FAN rather than a chain, and at 500 siblings only 21% of spots inherit — the delta shares along the chain and cannot see sibling identity, which is what a fan repeats. So for the shape the consumer is actually heading toward, the right tool is the list-level pooling Round 851 rejected on fragility, and THAT rejection is the one to revisit if memory pressure ever appears. Today it has not: the real store holds 4,654 lines, about 1.3 MB, and no consumer has reported a number.

THE HONEST SHAPE OF THIS ROUND. Nothing was built and one thing was learned that changes future work: the fork tree is already load-bearing UPSTREAM, so the read model is redundant rather than unguarded, and redundancy is a size question that wants a measurement no one has taken yet. The two doc comments that carried the wrong reason are corrected in place, because a right decision resting on a wrong reason is how the next round inherits the wrong reason.

It may not, and leaving a wrong reason under a right decision is how the next round inherits the wrong reason

THE DECISION STANDS ON A DIFFERENT REASON. A fact-id key would make this generator depend on a property of `MapLocator` in another crate — that nothing world-shaped reaches `LinePart` — which nothing at the generator boundary can check and which one added field upstream would break silently. The rendered-text key is LOCALLY exact and costs nothing: both pool to the same 882

THE DELTA MODEL IS SPECIFIED AND NOT BUILT. A world stores a spot only when it differs from what its fork parent answers; `lines()` walks up the chain and still returns `&[Line]`, so the API break Round 851 named as the blocker does not exist. Exact for any data — the fork-prefix property becomes a CHECK on the representation ("no owned spot before this world's fork point") rather than a precondition of it

THE TRIGGER FOR BUILDING IT IS NAMED: a consumer reporting real memory pressure on a CHAIN-shaped store. For a FAN-shaped one the delta model is the wrong tool and the answer is the list-level pooling Round 851 rejected — that rejection is the one to revisit, not this

NON-VACUOUS: 84 / 143 / 26,484 spots respectively DIFFER at or after the fork, so the forks are doing something

NOBODY HAS MEASURED A CONSUMER'S ACTUAL BRANCH COUNT AT ITS ACTUAL CONTENT. Every number above at more than nine branches comes from synthetic branches. The first honest scale measurement will come from the consumer's own store when their round-based design lands, not from here

THE DELTA MODEL, IF BUILT, CHANGES `ProjectionParts` — the baked `by_world` would carry owned spots only. It composes cleanly with the Round 851 pool (fewer spots to index) and nothing about it invalidates Round 851

THIS ROUND DID NOT ASK WHETHER `by_world` SHOULD BE BAKED FOR ALL WORLDS AT ALL. The consumer bakes every world-line so a fork door can switch worlds with no store read; whether a lazily materialised spot cache would serve that better is a different question and is not opened here

Round 854.decision_summary:
R854 (BUILD — the exclusion-integrity axis answered a whole-tree question from a Rust-only file set, and was therefore wrong in BOTH directions). Reported from the field by the external spec consumer, who migrated their codegen templates to the sigil citation form and watched Round 840 name seven Appendix-D sections as reachable only from an excluded tree. Every one of those seven IS cited in a scanned path and IS bound there. The report was false as stated, and it cost them real coverage: with no truthful prose form available for an Appendix D subsection, and 15506 generated citations as the alternative, they dropped the citation from the templates to get the gate green.

THE MECHANISM IS ONE FILTER. `scan_coverage` filtered all three of its sets to `.rs`, and `swallowed_citations` consumes two of them. The citation gate itself walks the configured paths with no extension filter at all — it reads C++ headers, Jinja templates, whatever a consumer enrols. So the detector's "still seen" side was a Rust-only view of a language-agnostic gate, and the doc comment stated the overclaim in as many words: cited nowhere the gate reads. Their control isolates it exactly: two Appendix-D sections stayed quiet under the identical setup, and the only thing separating those two from the seven is that they are additionally cited in a scanned RUST tree.

BOTH DIRECTIONS, FROM THE SAME FILTER, AND THE SECOND IS WORSE. False positive: cited in scanned C++ and in an excluded copy, reported as lost when the gate still reads it. False negative: cited ONLY in an excluded non-Rust file, which is precisely the coverage loss this axis exists to catch, and the axis could not see the file at all. A swallowed citation then reads as clean. The consumer reported the direction that shouted at them; the silent direction was ours to find.

A THIRD SYMPTOM, unreported and also live: `stale_exclusions` called an exclusion stale whenever it matched nothing in Rust, and a stale exclusion is a reject. A C++ consumer excluding a C++ tree was told to delete the declaration that was doing the work.

THE RUST-ONLY AXIS STAYS, AND IS NOW SAID OUT LOUD. Round 783 asks whether every Rust source is scanned or declared, and a language-agnostic version of that question would demand a declaration for every markdown and manifest file in the tree. So the counts stay Rust and the file SETS go language-agnostic, both derived from one walk so the two views cannot disagree about a file. The Round 840 question and the Round 783 question are different questions over the same tree, and only one of them is about Rust.

OUR OWN FIXTURES COULD NOT HAVE FOUND THIS, and one of them was already asserting the property while proving nothing. Every scan path in this repo held Rust only, so the filter was invisible by construction — and the Round 835 test that compares what the baseline gate covers against what the citation gate walks passed for exactly that reason: the two numbers were equal because there was no non-Rust file to disagree about. The fixture is now mixed-language, and that assertion is load-bearing for the first time.

THE CONSUMER'S PIN DECISION IS RIGHT AND ITS STATED RISK IS NOT. They are holding at the Round 840 revision because none of their three items had landed, which was true. But they cited a store-migration risk, and there is none in that range: `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` is 44 at both ends and no migration was added, so the bump they were weighing is migration-free. The gain was zero; the risk was zero too.

SSOT = this entry; their report is claudedocs/mnemosyne-field-report-r840-rust-only-scope.md in the consumer's tree.
changes_bullets: `scan_coverage` walks once and derives two views: the Round 783 counts stay Rust-only by design, while `scanned_files` and `excluded_files` hold every file the gate reads in any language — the order is reversed from before, where the `.rs` filter was applied at the walk and both views inherited it
`stale_exclusions` is language-agnostic: an exclusion over a C++ tree is doing work, and calling it stale told a consumer to delete a live declaration

`swallowed_citations` is now infallible and SKIPS a file it cannot read as UTF-8, exactly where the citation gate skips it — a signature that could not fail was returning a Result, and the new universe includes whatever binary a consumer's paths enrol

`validate-workspace` prints the file counts of the exclusion-integrity axis every run — gate files and excluded files, any language — because zero swallowed out of zero files read is the same clean a clean tree prints
the swallowed-citation failure message no longer carries fourteen spaces from a mis-wrapped format string
verification_bullets: THE FIXTURE WAS WRITTEN FIRST AND RUN AGAINST THE OLD CODE, and the old behaviour is exactly inverted: it reported `2.2`, cited in a scanned C++ file, and stayed silent about `8.8`, cited only in an excluded C++ file. Both worlds report a count of ONE, so a length assertion alone would have passed either way — the identity of the citation is what separates them
The third symptom was recorded the same way: an exclusion matching only a C++ tree was reported stale and failed the gate before the change

MEASURED ON THE CONSUMER'S FIVE WORKSPACES, on a copy in a scratch directory with the tool pin lifted, their tree read-only. The still-seen side read this many files before and after: mesh 0 then 57, scxml 106 then 430, wire 154 then 288, bytesguard and synth 193 then 946. The excluded side: mesh 1028 then 6314, wire 874 then 6091, scxml 922 then 2949, bytesguard and synth 835 then 2801. Their mesh ledger scanned ZERO Rust files, so its still-seen set was built from no files at all while the gate read 57

ALL FIVE STAY GREEN — zero swallowed citations before and after — so the change does not turn a consumer's passing gate red. Their current tree cannot reproduce the seven false positives because the citations were removed from the templates to get green, which is why the reproduction lives in a fixture

The Round 835 gate-equality assertion now compares the count of files the baseline gate READS against the citation gate's walk, and refuses to run unless that walk found a non-Rust file — previously it compared two numbers that were equal only because the fixture was all-Rust

Our own workspace is a near-no-op and the numbers say so: the gate side goes from 95 Rust to 100 files (five non-Rust under `studio/`), the excluded side from 122 to 135, and exclusion integrity stays 0
COST, absolute rather than a delta: the largest workspace — 6314 excluded files — takes 1.65s in a DEBUG build, so no delta measurement was needed to settle it

1288 workspace tests green under --no-fail-fast, +3 (two end-to-end, one over the coverage struct); clippy and fmt clean; validate-workspace exit 0 with T1=0 and T3 reject=0; validate-code-refs 0 violations
carry_forward_bullets: THE SYMBOL AXIS IS UNTOUCHED AND HAS THE SAME SHAPE OF HOLE. `lang_for_file` has no `.c` arm, so a C runtime gets file-level binding on its `.c` files and symbol-level on its `.h` files, silently, while `severity_binding = reject` reads as symbol-level enforcement. The consumer's C tree is 226 files with 139 hand-authored citations. Sharper than they reported it: `comment_syntax_for` in the SAME file does know `.c`, so this is an omitted arm rather than a considered scope

AND THE CONFIG KEY IS UNCHECKED, which is the workaround failing too: `[plugins.symbol_resolver.<lang>]` accepts any string, nothing verifies the dispatcher can ever produce that key, so a `c` or `kotlin` entry is parsed, registered, never consulted, and never mentioned. An unknown BACKEND warns; an unknown LANGUAGE does not

No symbol resolver ships for `go`, `kotlin` or `python` — the workspace carries tree-sitter-rust and tree-sitter-cpp only. Those trees bind file-level at best, which is a materially weaker claim than the C++ and Rust trees get. The consumer holds 181 / 235 / 194 hand-authored citations in them
A THIRD SITE OF THIS CLASS, found while reading and not fixed here: the fact and entity citation axis filters to `.rs` too, and unlike the coverage struct its doc comment says nothing about it

The Round 783 axis stays Rust-only, which for a consumer whose citations live in C++ means the coverage question they actually need — is every C++ source citing this ledger scanned — is not the one being asked. Their five workspaces satisfy it by declaring exclusions over Rust trees they never cite in
The Round 840 scoping limit carries unchanged: a citation of a section no ledger holds is invisible to this axis, in any language

Round 855.decision_summary:
R855 (BUILD — the symbol axis says which files it cannot reach, and reaches `.c` now). The second half of the field report Round 854 answered. The consumer's item was small and their diagnosis of the class was not: `lang_for_file` had no `.c` arm, so enrolling their C runtime — 226 files, 139 hand-authored citations — would have given the `.h` files symbol-level binding and the `.c` files beside them file-level, silently, under `severity_binding = reject`. They named the shape too: adding the arm is the small fix, and making an unreachable file LOUD is the one that closes the class.

THE OMISSION WAS VISIBLE IN THE SAME FILE. `comment_syntax_for`, one screen from `lang_for_file`, has always known `.c` — so the comment axis read those files while the symbol axis did not know what language they were. That is an omitted arm, not a considered scope, and the same disagreement covered case: one function lowercased the extension and the other did not, so a `.H` header was read by one and skipped by the other. The extension list is now a TABLE, the language set is DERIVED from it, and both functions agree about case.

LOUD MEANS COUNTED, NOT REJECTED. `symbol_axis_coverage` reports, every run, the files the axis reached (per language), the files whose language has no configured resolver, and the files whose extension maps to no language at all — each with the number of those files that carry a citation this ledger gates. That second number is the load-bearing one: a hundred unreachable files that cite nothing cost no coverage, and one that carries a gated citation is a symbol-level claim the run did not check. Rejecting instead would fail every workspace that enrols a directory holding a manifest or a markdown file, which is most of them; the defect was never that those files are unreachable, it was that nothing said so. Same shape as the Round 819 fact axis and the Round 783 coverage line: an axis that covers nothing prints the same silence as an axis where everything passed.

A DECLARED RESOLVER THAT CANNOT BE BUILT IS NOW A CONFIG ERROR. Two shapes, both previously silent-ish, both leaving `severity_binding = reject` reading as symbol-level enforcement the run does not perform. A `[plugins.symbol_resolver.c]` entry — the obvious workaround for a `.c` tree taking no symbol binding — parsed, registered, and was never consulted by anything, with no diagnostic at all. An unknown in-process backend printed to stderr and continued. Refusing cannot break a working config, because an entry this rejects was doing nothing by construction.

MEASURED ON THE CONSUMER'S FIVE WORKSPACES AND THE GAP IS NOT SMALL. Their synth ledger: 282 files that carry a gated citation are out of symbol reach — 96 Go, 92 SCXML, 81 Jinja templates, plus Kotlin, shell, text and schema files. Their bytesguard ledger: 8. Their mesh, wire and scxml ledgers: 0, because those ledgers' citations live in the C++ and Rust trees they do configure resolvers for. Before this round the tool reported none of that, and their `severity_binding = reject` read as symbol-level throughout.

AND THE COUNT WAS MISSING FROM THE ONE LINE THAT LISTS THE OTHERS. `symbol_mismatch` was counted into `violations: total` and named in the reject message but absent from the itemized summary, so the axis whose coverage depends on a resolver being configured was also the axis whose violation count a reader could not see. It is itemized now.

OUR OWN WORKSPACE CANNOT EXERCISE ANY OF THIS, and the new line said so the moment it existed: we configure NO symbol resolver at all, so 95 Rust files with 5 citing files take file-level binding under our own `severity_binding = reject`, and our five sections record seven bindings with ZERO symbols, so the axis would have nothing to check even with a resolver wired. Both halves of this round came from the field because dogfood here is structurally blind to them.

SSOT = this entry; their report is claudedocs/mnemosyne-field-report-r840-rust-only-scope.md in the consumer's tree.
changes_bullets: `SYMBOL_AXIS_EXTENSIONS` replaces the extension match: `.c` joins the cpp arm, the extension test is case-insensitive like `comment_syntax_for` beside it, and `symbol_axis_languages` derives the legal `[plugins.symbol_resolver.<lang>]` key set from the same table rather than restating it

`SetEqualityValidator::symbol_axis_coverage` — per language reached, per language with no configured resolver, per unmapped extension, each with files and gated-citation-carrying files; printed by `validate-code-refs` every run and carried in its JSON

`build_symbol_resolver_map` refuses an entry naming a language no extension maps to, or an in-process backend this build has no plugin for, instead of registering the first and warning about the second
`symbol_mismatch` is itemized in the `violations:` summary line and the JSON, where it was previously folded into the total only
SCHEMA_GUIDE documents the legal language keys, the shipped backends, and that an unreachable file binds at file granularity whatever `severity_binding` says
verification_bullets: THE `.c` FIX IS PROVEN BY THE MISMATCH PATH, not by the mapping: the existing C++ symbol-enforcement smoke gained a fourth case over a `.c` source, and its `stand_up` helper took an extension parameter so every C-family extension is reachable by the same fixture rather than one of them being assumed

INJECTION, applied to the table and reverted from a copy: removing the `("c", "cpp")` row turns the coverage assertion red and prints the pre-fix state as data — `unmapped_extensions: {"c": {files: 1, citing_files: 1}}`, the field-reported defect in one line

The coverage test discriminates all three destinations on one fixture (reached, mapped-but-unconfigured, unmapped) AND the citing half: an unreachable `.toml` reads `(1, 0)` while an unreachable `.md` carrying a citation reads `(1, 1)`, so a report that counted files instead of coverage would fail

The config refusal is asserted end-to-end through the binary in both shapes plus a CONTROL: a `symbol_resolver.c` key rejects, a `tree-sitter-kotlin` backend rejects, and the same fixture with a buildable `rust` entry exits 0 — so the two refusals are about the entries, not the fixture

MEASURED ON THE CONSUMER'S FIVE WORKSPACES, on a copy with the tool pin lifted, their tree read-only: synth 282 unreachable citing files (go 96, scxml 92, jinja2 81, kt 2, sh 5, txt 3, xsd 1, python 2), bytesguard 8 (scxml 4, sh 4), mesh and wire and scxml 0

NO NEW VIOLATION ON THEIR TREE: every workspace's `total` is fully accounted for by its itemized kinds, so symbol mismatches are 0 across all five. Their tree holds no `.c` file under any scan path and no uppercase C-family source, so both halves of the mapping change are inert there — they matter when the C runtime is enrolled, which is the ask

1292 workspace tests green under --no-fail-fast, +4 (two over the coverage struct and the derived language set, one `.c` end-to-end, one CLI refusal); clippy and fmt clean; validate-workspace exit 0 with T1=0 and T3 reject=0; validate-code-refs 0 violations
carry_forward_bullets: NO RESOLVER SHIPS FOR `go`, `kotlin` OR `python`. The extension table maps `.py` and `.go`, so those keys are legal and a consumer may configure them — but the workspace carries tree-sitter-rust and tree-sitter-cpp only, so an in-process entry for them is refused and the files stay file-level. `.kt` maps to nothing at all. The consumer holds 181 / 235 / 194 hand-authored citations in those three runtimes, and their synth ledger's 282 unreachable citing files are mostly this

The advisory stops at counting. It names extensions and languages, never the individual file, so a reader who wants the list must derive it — deliberate, because the useful next step is a resolver or a scan-path change, not a file-by-file audit

A THIRD SITE OF THE SAME CLASS IS STILL OPEN: the fact and entity citation axis filters to `.rs` with nothing in its doc comment saying so, so for a consumer whose facts are cited from C++ that axis is silently empty. Round 854 named it; this round did not close it

Our own workspace configures no resolver and records no symbol bindings, so every assertion here rests on fixtures plus the consumer's tree. Wiring a resolver into our own config would change nothing until our sections record symbols, which is a separate decision about how tightly this repo binds its own five sections

Round 856.decision_summary:
R856 (BUILD — the third site of the class, and a sweep that found the fourth). Round 854 closed the exclusion axis and Round 855 the symbol axis; both were reported from the field. This closes the one our own reading found: the fact and entity citation axis walked the configured paths and then filtered to `.rs`, and unlike the other two its doc comment did not even admit the filter — it said the scan boundary is "inherited, not invented", which was true of the directory rule it was describing and false of the file rule sitting three lines below it.

THE CLAIM IT PUBLISHES IS A COVERAGE CLAIM. `facts_cited` of `facts_total`, over `files_scanned`, reads as "these facts are cited somewhere in the code". Under a Rust-only universe that number is understated for any consumer whose citations live elsewhere, silently, and the axis prints it every run.

MEASURED ON THE STORE THIS AXIS WAS BUILT FOR, and the finding is not a hypothetical: the first playable consumer keeps its scenario files as `.scxml`, and those files carry HAND-AUTHORED fact citations in prose — `f-bell-counts`, `f-knots-are-sins`, `f-unconfessed-stays-bound`, `f-tide-slips`. The axis was blank in exactly the files where that author writes fact citations by hand. Files scanned 53 to 70, citing files 14 to 20, fact sites 37 to 49, distinct facts cited 23 to 28. Shape matches that name nothing in the store: 1 before, 1 after — ZERO new noise from the seventeen non-Rust files, so the widening bought coverage without buying a false-positive list.

NOISE STAYS BOUNDED BY WHAT WAS ALREADY THERE, not by an extension list: the namespace prefixes are DERIVED from the store's own key space and need two ids to exist at all, and the axis is advisory, so a shape match in data costs a printed line and never a red gate. That is the Round 819 design doing its job — this round did not weaken it, it stopped narrowing the universe underneath it.

THEN THE SWEEP, because fixing the third instance of a class and stopping is what the consumer's own field report warned about. Every extension-dependent branch in the citation source, read: the `is_rust` in `scan_coverage` is the documented Round 783 axis, the two `lang_for_file` sites are the symbol axis Round 855 made loud, and the last one was `comment_syntax_for`. `comment_only = true` reads comments only where a comment syntax is KNOWN and the whole text everywhere else, so the knob means two different things depending on the extension and nothing said which files got which. It is load-bearing in both directions — it is why the consumer's prose fact citations are read at all, and it is also why a citation-shaped token in a data file counts as a citation under a reject-level severity.

REPORTED, NOT CHANGED. Making unknown syntax scan nothing would have dropped the very prose citations this round just measured as real coverage. Round 857.decision_summary:
R857 (BUILD — the quest layer is consumable, and finding that out took being the consumer). The owner's cadence choice was the pinion side of the R568/R569 quest graph: is the fact→quest projection something a narrative runtime can actually wire against. So this round ran it the way that runtime would — against the first playable consumer's real store, asking the questions a quest layer asks — rather than reading the code and pronouncing.

THE FIRST COMMAND LIED, AND IT LIED WITH NUMBERS. `report-quest-graph --telling player` on that store printed 22 quests over 7 worlds with a per-world state column for each, `unresolved_quests: []`, and no complaint of any kind. Underneath, the manuscript walk had visited ZERO scenes in all 7 worlds. Run against the store's declared canon order the same command reports 117 done where the silent run reported 65, and 12 giver locators where it reported none. Every figure was wrong and every figure looked authoritative.

THE CAUSE IS AN OPTIONAL INPUT WITH A DEGENERATE DEFAULT. `resolve_canon_order_file` composes an EMPTY order when there is neither a `--order` flag nor a `[continuity].canon_order_path`, and a world-scoped read over an empty order is empty in every world. `playthrough_manuscript` already refuses a typo'd world — its own comment says a typo "must not read as an empty manuscript" — and a typo'd telling. This was the third and largest source of exactly that emptiness, and it was the unguarded one.

★THE FIRST FIX WAS WRONG AND THIS REPO'S OWN TESTS SAID SO. I put the refusal inside `playthrough_manuscript` and `payoff_coverage`, which broke `authoring_frontier` — the R596 surface whose PURPOSE is to name every scene that is not yet ordered, ratified by a test called `no_declared_order_is_not_an_incomplete_order`. An undeclared order is a defect for one question and the SUBJECT of another, and the guard belongs to the question, not to the math. So the rule sits in `world_scoped_inputs`, the shared preamble of the four report wrappers that serve a per-world question, and the frontier keeps calling the permissive projections directly.

WHAT THE CONSUMER ACTUALLY GETS, measured with the order declared: 22 quests, all giving-bound, 10 carrying prerequisites, `unresolved_quests` empty; 12 giver locators = 3 quests across 4 world-lines. That 3-of-22 is CORRECT and it names the authoring act a runtime depends on: exactly 3 of the 22 giving facts are disclosed in the `player` telling, the other 19 default to withhold, and R643 derives the locator seat from the fact's own canon coordinate — so putting a quest on the map is "disclose its giving fact in this telling", NOT "author a surface". No new substrate is needed for the quest layer; the pull R562 registered is satisfied.

AND ONE HONEST HOLE IN THE STATE AXIS: across 22 quests × 7 worlds, the real store yields 117 done and 37 unknown and ZERO open. Four world-lines complete every quest; the three ending-lines complete some. That is faithful — these are finished manuscripts, not save-states — but it means the `open` verdict, the one a quest LOG would render, has no real-data instance anywhere. A consumer building an active-quest panel has nothing to test against yet.

SSOT = this entry.
changes_bullets: `check_order_declared` (mnemosyne-validate::continuity) — a world-scoped read over a canon order with no nodes is refused when the store holds sections, with the section and fact counts and both declaration sites named in the message

`world_scoped_inputs` (mnemosyne-ops) — the shared store-plus-order preamble of the four report wrappers that answer a per-world question (payoff coverage, playthrough manuscript, playable world, quest graph), with the refusal applied once so a new wrapper inherits it
the inner projections stay permissive, because `authoring_frontier` composes them to answer the opposite question and its two tests hold that decision
verification_bullets: MEASURED ON THE FIRST PLAYABLE CONSUMER'S LIVE STORE, on a copy, theirs read-only: without the order, 7 worlds with 0 scenes, 65 done, 0 locators, exit 0 and no warning; with the order, 117 done, 37 unknown, 12 locators, exit 0. After this round the first form exits 1 naming 66 sections and 1106 facts, and the second is byte-unchanged

THE REFUSAL AND THE EXCEPTION ARE ASSERTED ON ONE FIXTURE, all four world-scoped wrappers plus the frontier: each wrapper's message must name both the state and the repair AND the counts it would have skipped, the frontier must still list the unordered scene, and a CONTROL declares a single edge so the same fixture answers — proving the refusal is about the empty declaration, not about the fixture

★The first cut of this fix put the guard in the two inner projections and turned two existing ops tests red — `authoring_frontier_flags_unordered_scenes_when_order_absent` and `no_declared_order_is_not_an_incomplete_order`. That is the round's sharpest evidence: a vacuity guard is a claim about which question is being asked, and this repo had already ratified the other answer

The 3-of-22 locator figure was chased to its cause rather than assumed: 3 of the 22 giving facts carry a `player` override with `mode: state`, the other 19 default to withhold. An earlier guess of mine — that the author had surfaced no giving facts — was wrong twice over and each correction came from reading the store, not from reasoning about it
1294 workspace tests green under --no-fail-fast, +1; clippy and fmt clean; validate-workspace exit 0 with T1=0 and T3 reject=0; validate-code-refs 0 violations

Every consumer pipes a long report into a pager, and this round's own first measurement read that 101 as a defect in the report before recognising it as the pipe. Not fixed here: the repair is process-level (restore the default SIGPIPE disposition), it changes the exit code of every verb, and it deserves its own round

The only store that ever authored quest-giver SURFACES — the R562 dnd-quest experiment — no longer loads: R708 removed the `{kind:value}` object shape and its migration is deliberately manual, so that store needs 18 facts and 5 predicates re-authored. The map seam's end-to-end demonstration therefore has no loadable fixture, and the live store exercises it only through R643's derived seat
`open` has no real-data instance: 117 done, 37 unknown, 0 open across 22 quests × 7 worlds. The verdict a quest log renders is the one no store has yet produced, so it rests on unit fixtures alone

The refusal is scoped to the four world-scoped wrappers. `validate-continuity` and `report-timeline-gaps` still read an undeclared order and report `order_nodes: 0` beside `sections`, which is the honest alternative for a gate — but the split now has to be maintained by hand, and a fifth world-scoped verb that does not route through `world_scoped_inputs` would reopen the hole

Round 858.decision_summary:
R858 (DEBT, code 0 — Round 840's positive control was four false positives, and the audit trail says otherwise until this entry). The external spec consumer adopted R854 and R855, bumped its pin to `5bbf4d17`, and opened its report by withdrawing the evidence it had given us a round earlier. That withdrawal invalidates a claim in OUR ledger, so this entry states the correction in prose — the ledger is append-only and R840's own text cannot be edited.

WHAT R840 CLAIMS. Its decision summary says the fixed detector "takes it to zero on their fixed config and to exactly four — `wire-W1`, `W3`, `W4`, `W5` — on the pre-fix config", and its verification bullet reports that same four as measured on the consumer's own wire ledger. It was presented as the positive control: a detector only ever seen returning 0 proves nothing, so we forced it non-zero before trusting the 0.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE. Those four sections are cited in SCANNED C++ all along, so nothing was ever swallowed and the correct answer for that config is 0. VERIFIED HERE, not taken on report: `§wire-W1` is cited in 3 files under the wire ledger's scanned C++ trees, `W3` in 5, `W4` in 7, `W5` in 3 — the consumer's own counts, reproduced by grep against their tree read-only. Round 859.decision_summary:
R859 (DEBT — every report verb died at exit 101 when its reader stopped early, and Round 857 recorded that as a carry rather than paying it). The debt was found by being the consumer: `report-quest-graph … | head -3` exits 101 with `failed printing to stdout: Broken pipe (os error 32)`, and in R857 I first read that 101 as a defect in the report I was measuring. Every consumer pipes a long report into `head` or a pager, so this was on every report verb, not on one.

THE CAUSE IS IN THE RUNTIME, NOT IN THE REPORTS. Rust installs `SIG_IGN` for `SIGPIPE` before `main`, so a write to a closed pipe returns `EPIPE` instead of terminating the process, and `println!` unwraps that error. Nothing in this codebase asked for that; it is the default every Rust binary starts with, and it is wrong for a CLI whose whole job is printing.

ONE SITE, NOT A PRINT HELPER. `main`'s first statement restores the default disposition, so the process ends by signal 13 the way `cat` and `grep` do. The alternative — an `EPIPE`-aware print wrapper — would have to be adopted by every one of the hundreds of `println!` calls here and in the ops/query crates, and the next one added would reopen the hole. A disposition covers writes that do not exist yet; a helper covers the ones someone remembered.

THE UNSTABLE ROUTE WAS TRIED FIRST AND IS NOT AVAILABLE: `#[unix_sigpipe = "sig_dfl"]` does not compile on stable 1.94 under either spelling. So the fix is one `libc::signal` call, and `libc` becomes a unix-gated dependency of the CLI — no new vendored crate (0.2.186 was already in `Cargo.lock` through the dev-dependency chain), one declared edge.

WHY ONLY THIS BINARY. `mnemosyne-mcp` speaks a stdio protocol and `mnemosyne-server` speaks HTTP; terminating mid-write there truncates a frame a peer is parsing. A CLI report is the case where dying like `cat` IS correct — the reader asked to stop. Neither of the other binaries is touched.

SAFETY IS A POSITION, NOT A HOPE. The call is sound at exactly that point: `main`'s first statement, before any output, in a binary that spawns no thread. The disposition then governs every pipe the process writes, which is only its own stdout and stderr — it opens no socket (verified: zero matches for any socket or async runtime type in the CLI), and its one child, `git log` read through `Command::output`, is never written to. All three facts were checked rather than assumed, because a process-wide signal change is only as narrow as the process is.

★AND THE FIX NARROWS THE PIPE CASE ONLY, WHICH IS THE HALF THAT COULD HAVE GONE WRONG. Making write failures silent would be a worse defect than the panic: a report that gets truncated by a full disk must say so. Measured against `/dev/full`, which fails every write with `ENOSPC`: the panic and the 101 both stay. That control is now a permanent test, compile-gated to Linux rather than skipped at run time — a runtime skip would read as a pass on a platform where the control never ran.

SSOT = this entry.
changes_bullets: `restore_default_sigpipe` in the CLI's `main`, first statement, unix-gated: one `libc::signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_DFL)` with the safety position stated as a doc section (single-threaded at that point, no socket, no child stdin)
`libc` as a `[target.'cfg(unix)'.dependencies]` edge of `mnemosyne-cli` — already in `Cargo.lock`, so the lockfile gains one line and no crate
`tests/sigpipe_smoke.rs` — the closed-reader outcome, plus the `/dev/full` control that keeps a real write failure loud
`mnemosyne-mcp` and `mnemosyne-server` deliberately unchanged: a truncated protocol frame is not an improvement on a panic
verification_bullets: THE TEST WAS WRITTEN FIRST AND RUN AGAINST THE UNFIXED BINARY, where it fails exactly as the field case does: exit 101 with `failed printing to stdout: Broken pipe (os error 32)` on stderr
INJECTION, applied then reverted from a copy: deleting the one call from `main` turns the test red again with that same message, so the assertion rests on the fix and not on the fixture

NON-VACUITY IS ASSERTED, NOT ASSUMED: the fixture report must exceed 65,536 bytes, because a report that fits in the pipe buffer lets the child finish every write before the reader closes — and then the test would pass against an unfixed binary. 9,000 sections put it over the line, and the assertion names the byte count when it does not

THE ORIGINAL FIELD CASE, RE-RUN: `report-quest-graph --telling player --order canon-order.json | head -3` on a copy of the consumer's store now prints its three lines with an EMPTY stderr and a producer status of 141 (128+13), where before it printed a panic
BOTH NEIGHBOURING PATHS ARE UNCHANGED, checked on the same store: the same command without a pipe still exits 0, and the R857 refusal (no canon order declared) still exits 1 with its message
NO HOOK OR SCRIPT REGRESSES: every pipeline under `.githooks/` and `scripts/` runs over `printf`, `git diff` or a log file, never over CLI stdout, so nothing that uses `pipefail` can now see a 141

carry_forward_bullets: The two sibling binaries keep the panic. For `mnemosyne-mcp` a closed stdout is the client hanging up mid-session, and the right answer there is probably a clean shutdown rather than either a panic or a signal death — unbuilt, and it needs a protocol-level decision rather than a disposition

Death by signal means no destructor runs. Nothing in the CLI's print path holds a lock or a temp file that a `Drop` must clean, so there is nothing to lose today; a future verb that streams a report while holding a write lock would need to know this

The exit code of a piped report is now 141 rather than 101. Both are failures to a naive `$?` check, so no caller that was already correct changes behaviour — but a caller that special-cased 101 would need to know, and none exists in this repo

Round 860.decision_summary:
R860 (DEBT — my Round 856 report line counted files the gate cannot read, and the config key named after exclusion does not exclude. Both found by the external spec consumer; one of them is a correction to something I asserted about their tree without measuring it.)

★FIRST, THE CORRECTION THAT IS MINE. My Round 858 reply told them that their 489 whole-read template and scenario files "carry no section-shaped token, so they are quiet". They measured: synth holds 462 own-namespace tokens, bytesguard 4, wire 0. I re-measured before writing this and the direction is theirs — my own raw regex over their whole-read files finds 525 in synth and exactly 4 in bytesguard, differing from their 462 only by counting method, not by fact. Their ledgers ARE quiet, but for the opposite reason to the one I gave: not "no tokens" but tokens present, resolving, and already bound. That changes the risk description — the exposure is not dormant, it is active and handled, and the next fixture carrying a NON-resolving token fails immediately rather than someday. This is the second time I have asserted an unverified measurement about a consumer's tree, in the same round I thanked them for verifying before writing.

THE R856 LINE OVERSTATED ITS OWN AXIS. It reported, on their first run, `1138 of 1684 scanned file(s) … read whole {"class": 368, "pyc": 23, "bin": 10, "jar": 1}` — and the citation scan does `read_to_string` and skips whatever is not valid UTF-8, so every one of those compiled artifacts is walked and then dropped. No axis ever saw them. The count named the wrong files and inflated the exposure, and it did so in the line whose whole purpose is to say which files the gate reads whole. The split is now MEASURED — the same `read_to_string` question the gate asks, asked of the same file — rather than inferred from an extension, and the unreadable ones get their own advisory because a configured path full of build output is a real finding about the config.

★AND THAT MAKES THE NUMBER STABLE WITHOUT A HAND LIST, which is their sharper framing: "a number that differs between a developer and CI is not a measurement." Their counts depended on whether the reader had built the project, because `paths` enrolled parent directories holding `build/` and `__pycache__/`. The fix here excludes a binary artifact by the UTF-8 property it inherently lacks, not by a directory name on a skip list — and this codebase's every hand list has drifted (R777, R783). Adding `build/` to the walk's skip names was considered and REFUSED: `build` is a legitimate source directory name, and a false negative there hides real citations, which is worse than the noise it removes.

THE ONE THING THEY ASKED FOR: `scan_exclusions` DOES NOT EXCLUDE FROM THE READ SET. `paths` is the only thing that decides what the gate reads. `scan_exclusions` declares intent for the Round 783 coverage axis and feeds the Round 840 excluded set. So an entry naming a subtree that a `paths` entry already covers matches real files, reports NO stale exclusion, and changes nothing — which is config that looks like it works. Their first fix was exactly that, and only a diff of the counts showed it; they reverted and narrowed `paths` instead. REPRODUCED HERE on a copy of their scxml ledger: adding `sce/src/runtime/` to `scan_exclusions` leaves the gate reading 444 files and reporting 96 violations, unchanged, with `stale exclusions: 0`.

THE OVERLAP IS NOW LOUD, AND ADVISORY RATHER THAN A REJECT. A file in both sets says two things at once and the exclusion is the half that cannot win, so it is a contradiction worth naming — but no existing consumer's gate is weakened by it, and a check that fires on a workspace which has been correct for rounds is the check the next person switches off. So it names the count, three files, and the repair.

WHAT WAS NOT BUILT, deliberately: a key that subtracts a subtree from the read set. Narrowing `paths` already expresses it, explicitly, and giving `scan_exclusions` that second meaning would silently un-gate citations for any consumer who had used it in its declaring sense.

Round 861.decision_summary:
R861 (DEBT — a delegation instruction read by the delegate has a floor, and three of the four things standing on that floor were wrong). Filed by the first playable consumer, whose commits and pushes were all blocked after they adopted `[tool] pin`: a concurrent session put an older binary back on PATH sixty-five minutes later, and every command that reads a config then told them their config was wrong.

WHAT WAS ALREADY OURS, so the round does not re-decide it. Round 828 documented the parse trap, including the circularity that a pin naming a pre-`[tool]` revision names the one binary that cannot read it, and measured it on two real consumer binaries — one of them the very build in this report. Round 840 corrected the floor to "the newest key in your file". Neither is superseded here.

WHAT IS NEW IS THAT THE FLOOR IS A STANDING PROPERTY, NOT AN ADOPTION STEP. Round 828's remedy is an ordering — upgrade, install, confirm `--version`, then declare — and this consumer followed it. The older binary arrived after the ordering was finished, which no ordering discipline reaches. So the guidance now says to resolve the tool by something that names one revision, because a name on PATH is whatever was installed last.

THE ESCAPE HATCH WAS DOCUMENTED AS UNCONDITIONAL AND HAS A FLOOR OF ITS OWN. `MNEMOSYNE_PIN_SKIP` is read inside `enforce_tool_pin`, which runs only after `parse_config` has returned, so a build that cannot parse the file never reaches the waiver. Measured on the reported binary: the waived run and the unwaived run produce the identical parse error. An escape hatch below the floor it exists to escape is not one, and the guide said otherwise.

THE DIAGNOSTIC THEY ASKED FOR CANNOT EXIST IN THE FORM THEY ASKED FOR IT. Their recommendation was a special message for when the unknown top-level key is `tool`; that message could only ever ship inside a build that already knows `tool`, and such a build never emits "unknown field `tool`". It would be dead the day it landed. The live form is the general one, and this round builds that: any unknown key now carries this build's own revision and the rule that a config is readable only by a Mnemosyne at or after the revision that introduced its newest key. It cannot help the binary in the report — a build too old to know a key is also too old to carry the sentence explaining it — so it is written for the key that does not exist yet.

THE REPORT'S ONE FACTUAL ERROR, AND THE REAL DEFECT UNDERNEATH IT. They wrote that nothing checks whether the build at `$MN_ROOT/<pin>/bin` is the revision that path names. Round 832's loop guard does check, and it was measured doing so: with a current build installed at a mis-named path, the refusal names the broken install and gives the reinstall line. But the check is performed BY THE REPLACEMENT, and the class of replacement that most needs checking is the one least able to check. With a pre-`[tool]` build at that same path the only message is `mnemosyne.toml parse failed` — the same misdirection this whole report is about, emitted from inside the mechanism meant to prevent it. So the check moves BEFORE the hand-off: the switch asks the installed build which revision it is, and refuses when the answer is a different revision or is missing.

ASKING FIRST NEEDED A QUESTION EVERY BUILD ANSWERS, AND ONE BINARY DID NOT. `--version` is that question — Round 286 called it a universal surface — and it is also the ONLY command that survives on a build too old to parse the workspace config, which is measured here rather than assumed. `mnemosyne-render` never had one. That cost nothing while a binary's revision was something only a human read; it stopped costing nothing the moment another binary began asking. The test derives the binary set from cargo, so the next binary owes an answer the day it exists.

ROUND 840 FIXED A DOUBLED SUBJECT AND CREATED ONE. It gave `PinRefusal::Different` a subject of its own so the refusal would stop repeating the pin; the sibling caller in `switch_to_pinned` supplies a subject too, so every switchable refusal has since printed `note: this build this build is ...`. Found by reading the note during this round's own measurements, and reported by nobody.

WHAT IS NOT BUILT, AND WHY. Their recommendation (B) — a permanently ignored namespace so a future launcher directive cannot poison parsing — is REFUSED as stated: it converts a loud refusal into a silent unenforced run, which is precisely the outcome Rounds 825 and 826 chose fail-closed to avoid, and a top-level catch-all would also destroy the typo detection Round 828 names as deliberate. Their recommendation (A) — a separate launcher whose contract is frozen — is the only one of the three that reaches the reported incident, and it is a design question rather than an edit. It is Round 862.

Round 862.decision_summary:
R862 (DESIGN — the floor moves because delegation is read AFTER validation, not because the launcher and the tool are one binary). Round 861 answered the consumer's report and left their recommendation (A) standing: split the launcher into a separate artifact whose contract is frozen, as rustup is to rustc. This round answers it. (A) is the right diagnosis of a symptom and the wrong cut — what has to be separated is the ORDER, not the artifact.

THE MECHANISM, stated precisely because Round 840 recorded the consequence as though it were inherent. `load_config` reads the file, hands it to `parse_config`, which deserialises the whole document into `WorkspaceConfig` under `deny_unknown_fields`, and only then calls `enforce_tool_pin`.
